The Times does not approve of this move-
ment, which had not, at this inaugural
step, sufficient countenance from members
of Parliament; and only dealt in the
question of electoral re-adjustment with
admitted anomalies which time will correct.—
But in truth, the Conference did much more
than this. It dealt with the extension of the
suffrage to agricultural labourers, which, in
itself, is an exceedingly important question,
as well as in the strong, indirect influence it is
sure to have on the labourers' social condition.
Our reformers, in contemplating the work that
lies before them, should not for a moment lose
sight of the fact that the support of the news-
paper press will be sure to come to them if
they make their proceedings practical and
effective. The Times understated the numbers
present at the meeting, and misrepresented
other matters connected with it; but, notwith-
standing this, it was evidently convinced that
there was a serious purpose in view, which
may not be lost sight of, and which is likely
enough to be worked out.
The real duty of those who have taken this
work in hand dues not lie in reconciling slight
differences of opinion or plan. These are
necessary; in fact, cannot be avoided. No
abuse ever existed upon the character of which
those who opposed it were in precise agree-
ment; nor has any change ever been made
unaccompanied by many suggestions differing
from each other as to the best remedy. Plans
of political reform have never been any ex-
ception to this rule; but when they have been
made the subject of public discussion, the
best is carried, or a complex plan is contrived
out of the good points of several; and in this
way the present movement will take definite
shape, and win general approval and support.
And when it has worked itself into this
position, the Times will, in accordance with
its old and invariable custom, give it the ad-
vantage of its support.
What is now required is to get as speedily
as possible before the public; to state broadly
and ,plainly what is meant to be agitated
for. A popular political creed, accepted pretty
generally by the constituencies, would have a
wonderful effect in widening the views and
stimulating the courage of Parliamentary
candidates. It is absolutely necessary that the
Liberal party, or those of them at least who
really mean progress, should have a set of
questions prepared before the next general
election takes place by which candidates may
be tested, and upon their answers to which
they may be accepted or rejected. The Go-
vernment must be lea to see that the active
reformers of the country are in earnest; Mr.
Gunstorm and his colleagues should be com-

means finished, and that in anything they

ELECTORAL REFORII CONFERENCE. 1
Tun conference called by the Electoral
Reform Association on Tuesday last at St.
James's Hall may be regarded as a decided
success. The attendance was numerous, the
spirit good, and the practioal oonclusions,
affirmedby resolution, though not all-inclusive,
were of the right kind.
The facts contained in the various papers
read, and the statements of several of the
speakers make out an overwhelming case in
favour of a " readjustment " of our consti-
tuencies, so as to secure a more equitable
system of representation, and if such a reform
be not secured by vigorous action within a
reasonable time, the fault will lie at the door
of those who have taken the matter up as
leaders. The motion as to the assimilation of
the county and borough franchise, as a matter
to pass into the new programme, was en-
thusiastioally received by the meeting, and
we may rest satisfied that in its discussion
information will be elicited, and an active
political life excited in the agricultural
labourer which will tend strongly to lift him
from his present political and social degrada-
tion. The wicked " agitator, '' so much dreaded
and so much talked about by farmers, land-
lords, nobles, and bishops, may now any day
make his appearance, not simply to urge an
advance in wages on grounds of justice and
humanity, but to insist on the political ad-
vanoement of the people, to demand on their
behalf the right to vote, that by their political
power and influence they May enforce higher
conditions of existence than they now enjoy,
and a better %manatee, in the law for the
comfort and security of their lives.
Ever since the agricultural labourers began
their " agitation " for increased wages, there
have been ridiculously exaggerated cries of
fear from country [gentlemen, dignitaries of
the Church, and stupid members of Parlia-
ment on the stump. They have been trying
to persuade us that, on the whole, the agri-
cultural labourers' condition was rather to
be envied than pitied, and that although in
certain particulars some few slight improve-
ments might be desirable, still all that needed
doing could be done easily and speedily if the
tg agitator " would bat keep away, and allow
the labourer and the farmer to settle the matter
between them. This game at make-believe is
now we hope about being brought to an
end. The labourer in our fields is about to be
invited into the ranks of English Freemen.
Whatever strength of speech, or vigour of
action may be necessary, must be used by the
men of the new agitation to effect this
purpose; and if horse-ponds, or any kind of
rough horse-play should be resorted to by the
farmers or their friends to prevent this, what-
ever disagreeable omequenoea may fellow

good sense, and the honest disposition of the
working people to destroy abuses and get rid
of anomalies in everything connected with
our law and its administration, as well as with
our representgtive system. They may secure
the support of the most obtrusive and extreme
easily enough; but, unless they can also
reach and draw to them the quiet multitudes
beyond these, and to whom such noisy persons
are as units to thousands, their efforts will
end in failure. And in the 'interest of re-
form, so much needed in so many ways, it is
very undesirable that this should be the case.
LLOYD JONES.

TH.E Bishop of GLOUCESTER, of " horse-

of the ATTORNEY- GENERAL at Exeter, who
referred to the words used by the bishop in.

search of better wages; that is, from places

places where they were higher, and to combine
for the same purpose, or to better his condition.
Always allowing that there were two sides to
every question, only protesting against the

The Blsnor complains of "being slandered,

Man," said he, in the hope that he would be

hood, which the &snot) himself denies, for he

and he gives a Latin .cinotation, which he

where could be the slander? The use of

Tun controversy between Mr. 11A.unrsort

I may add that from the first I was con-

own mind, but when a modern reformer so
sincere and able as Mr. HARRISON uses such
very ugly phrases, we must not be surprised if
the out women of the world scream and cry
" spoliation " in a very alarming manner.
This is a matter worth hearing in mind when
those Who labour as reformers speak of each
other's intentions and efforts.
• I Cannot answer the demands made on me
by Mr. HARRISON as to definitions of co-
• operation in system and purpose. I have my
own views as to how co-operation will most
likely develop° itself as a system. I regard
all experiments now going on merely as tenta-
tives, hopeful as efforts in the right direction
some carrying with them more than others of
scientific form, and of that wise generosity of
spirit which Mr. HAnursox has failed as yet
to discover sufficiently in this movement. I also
wish Mr. HARRISON to remember as a mere per-
sonal item in our argument, that when I spoke
of an annual 15 millions profit on the pur-

chases of working men, I did not mention it
as a realizable sum ; I simply put it to show
him how incorrect his own statement was;
to the effect that if all the workers in England
were in co-operation their condition as workers
might be no better than it is. I was dis-
proving his hypothesis, not reasoning out a
proposition of my own. The question as
to whether co-operation will give better
Wages, I answer without hesitation, Yes,—
most emphatically, yes, ---- simply because

make all workers partners, and therefore par-

ing to pay bonus on wages where no money
investment has been made, and in certain
cases has succeeded.
Of the:Double-Shift system not another word
need be said. In special trades under excep-
tional circumstances it may be introduced, but
not in our staple industries. Common sense,
however, and. the logic of facts must settle
this matter, not theoretic expectations, or the
logic of words.

articles.title: LLOYD SONES.
articles.text:
LLOYD SONES.

EDUCATION FOR THE NEW SYSTEM.
IN proceeding to describe the way in which
the transformation of character will be pro-
duced which is necessary for the realization
of the new system, the first point which de-
mands consideration is the nature of this
transformation. It will be first intellectual,
and, then moral. Intellectually, it will be a
'ohange from ignorance and erroneous ideas in
reference to the causes of evil and of good—
an unenlightened and very defective intellec-
tual state—to the knowledge of these causes,
or true enlightenment.
In this change both our truths will be
illustrated (see BEE-HtvE, Nov. 9): There
mast be a cause for the acquirement of the
new knowledge, namely, that it has been dis-
covered and described, that the person who
acquires it has the necessary mental suscepti-
bilities and powers, arid that it is brought
under his notice. And. the person who
acquires it must be mentally active in doing
so. It will not be "given him independently
of himself;" that is, independently of any
mental efforts of his. His new opinions or
knowledge will not be formed "for him, and
not by him," And he willform the determina-
tion to examine into the subject. But he
will be causal to form it.
By examining the facts of the subject the
student in his new field of investigation will
be enabled to perceive the causes which have
produced the very defective characters which
lib's° hitherto been universal, and how very
defective, intellectually and morally, the best
characters which have hitherto existed have
necessarily been. I will first state the chief
of these causes, and the intellectual change,
and will then speak of their effects, and the
moral change.
First, as to the causes and the intellectual
change. The student in this new field will see
that men have not known the injurious effects
in man's character and conduct which are pro,-
duced by ignorance and erroneous ideas in
reference to the causes of evil and of good;
that they have not even known their own
ignorance and the ignorance of society upon
this subject; and that they have not under-
stood the demoralizing effects of the divided
and opposing interests and the inequalities of
general education and condition which are
the fundamental characteristics of the present
system, and are the natural effects of the de-
teriorated characters which are caused by this
ignorance and these erroneous ideas, and must
be continued so long as these inferior charac-
ters are formed in all, as they have hitherto
been. And he will perceive that men have
known nothing of the humanizing influence or
effects of the knowledge of the causes of evil
and of good; and of the necessity for union
and co-operation in all the business of life,
and for equality of general education, and
equality of condition according to ago, to satisfy
the enlightered social love which will exist in
characters humanized by the new knowledge;
and how powerfully influential, as causes of
good, these institutions will be, within suit-
able arrangements, and when men have
acquired the intellectual and moral character
to which these social conditions will be suited.

And he will become aware that the defective
formation of character in children is the effect

in part of the influences of persons ignorant
and in error in reference to the causes of evil

and of good, and whose characters, therefore,
have been very defectively formed, and in

part of the injurious arrangements, institu-
tions, and general proceedings of the pre-
sent state of society; and that in more ad-
vanced life this effect is confirmed by the

ignorance in reference to the causes of evil
and of good in which the individuals have
been caused to remain, and the erroneous
ideas in reference to them which they have
been caused to acquire, arid by the continuance
of the injurious external influences of the pre-
sent system. He will perceive that in early
life the individuals are chiefly influenced from
without; and that in more advanced life they
are still very powerfully influenced by external
causes, but that they are also influenced very
powerfully by the • ideas and the habits of
feeling and action which they have been
caused to acquire. And he will see that by
acquiring the new knowledge the injurious
influences of the ignorance and the erroneous
ideas in reference to the causes of evil and. of
good will be removed, and the beneficial in-
fluences of true ideas upon these subjects will
be substituted for them; and that by this
change the individuals will become impervious
to many of the injurious external influences
of the present system. Those who have ac-
quired the new knowledge will not be deceived
by the erroneous opinions of. others, as they
were before, and will have feelings of con-
tempt for many ideas and proceedings which
they viewed with approval and respect while
they were ignorant and in error upon this

subject; contempt for the ideas, but not for
the persons who have them; for they will
know that all are caused to acquire the
opinions which they do acquire. The dis-
torting medium of ignorance and erroneous
ideas through which they have hitherto

viewed. the -prooeedinga of the human race

will be removed, and they will see clearly
the folly and absurdity which, while men have
been ignorant of the causes of evil and of
good, have necessarily characterised the con-

duct of individuals and societies in all that has
been done to form the character and to
promote the happiness of the population, of
all classes, and in the pursuit -of in-
dividual happiness. And they will see
clearly the means by which every fairly
organized ohild may be edueated to acquire a
character of true enlightenment and enlight-
ened goodness, and by which all may be
placed in delightful surroundings, and may
have every reasonable want abundantly
supplied. This will be the intellectual trans-
formation produced by the acquirement of the
knowledge of the causes of evil and of good.
By this change the chief cause of evil, the
ignorance and erroneous ideas upon this
subject, will be superseded by the chief cause
of good, the knowledge of these causes. And
this change, which will be an internal sub-
stitution of the chief causes of good, for the
ohief cause of evil, in those who acquire the
new knowledge, will be the substitution of
external causes of good for external causes of
evil to those who are influenced by the indivi-
duals in whom the transformation is produced.
For to all who are influenced by them the
changed individuals will become external
causes of good, instead of b3ing causes of evil,
as of necessity they were, more or less, but
always to a great extent, while they were
ignorant upon this subjeot.

Second, as to the 'effects of these CaU36.4.
The moral transformation will be equally
extensive. When men know the causes which
have produced the defeats of character which
have hitherto existed and which now exist
(speaking of the fairly organized. races of men),
they will know that it is unjust to be angry,
and harsh, und vindictive, or to be in any way
unkind; and, in due time, when this know-
ledge has influenced them sufficiently, those
who are already sufficiently intelligent and
well disposed will cease to have these de-
moralising feelings. Instead of the ,ideas
which have caused men to be irritable,
irascible, unkind, vindictive, and selfish
(the erroneous supposition that men are
themselves the primary causes of their

Nov. 16, 1872.

qualities and acts, and the consequent ex-
aggerated ideas of moral responsibility,
see BEE-HIVE, Nov. 9), they will have ideas
upon those subjects which will cause them to
feel kindly towards all, and to desire earnestly
that the rational happiness of every individual
should be promoted to the utmost possible ex-
tent. They will know that those who have
acquired any of the defective characteristics
which alone have been acquired by all classes
in the present state of society, however mis-
taken or bad they may be, would have
acquired a character of true enlightenment
and enlightened goodness if they had been in-
fluenced from birth by the favourable condi-
tions of the new system in persons and things.
And this knowledge will continually excite
rationally their benevolent instincts,
.instead
of the constant irrational excitement of their
instincts of combativeness and malevolence,
previously produced in them by the erroneous
ideas. They will have for a time more or less
difficulty in subduing the old habits of in-
jurious feeling which they had been caused to
acquire while they were ignorant of the causes
of evil and of good to man; but they will be
enabled to do so by recurring 'continually to
the thoughts of the causes which ;have pro-
duced whatever may be displeasing to them in
their fellow men. These thoughts will excite
in them intelligently considerate and kiud
feelings, instead of the ignorant feelings of
unkindness and anger which were excited by
the erroneous ideas. The new knowledge will
cause these new thoughts to arise continually ;
and when they do so it will not be difficult to
keep up the thoughts; and by keeping them up,
the good feelings will be excited and
strengthened, and the bad .ones will be
weakened and subdued. And thus in due
time a moral transformation will be produced,
in those who are sufficiently intelligent and
:well disposed, which never can occur while
men are ignorant of the causes of evil and of

good.
And, again, in the producing of this moral
transformation our two truths will be exempli-
fied. The individual in whom it °ours will
have been caused to acquire the improved
character, and to make the mental efforts
necessary for acquiring it; but it will be to a
great extent the afoot of his own mental
efforts. Neither the change nor the determi-
nations which preceded the efforts neoessary to
produce it will have been, "formed for him
and not by him." But his agency, although
it will have been a necessary part ;of the
entire cause of the change, will not have been
the primary cause of it. If the causes, in
himself and external to him, which produced
his agency, had not existed, the :determina-
tions, and the efforts, and the consequent
change, would not have been produced.
But it is not only in the development, of
man's moral nature that the beneficial effects
of the new knowledge will be experienced.
This knowledge, while thus producing the
enlightened desire for the promotion of the
rational happiness of all to the utmost pos-
sible extent, and the other social feelings
which are necessary for individual and general
well-being, will at the same time enable those
who acquire it to construct the social arrange-
ments which are necessary, in conjunction
with the improved character, for the practical
realisation of the object of their aspirations,
and to carry out the Change from the old to
the new system beneficially for all.
There is more that is highly important to
be said upon this subje3t.

HENRY TWIS.

P.S. I shall have pleasure in replying next
week to Mr. HAILILISON'S questions, so far as
they apply to Social Co-operation. Mr. JONES
Will no doubt speak for co-operative trading.
It is a mistake to say that I "look upon it
merely as the old social abomination." I
spoke of it as "in the midst of the abonii-
uation.s of the existing system.

There was another meeting of publicans
on Monday at the Holborn MUSie Hall to con-
sider the course adopted by Colonel Hender-
son with regard to the granting of exemption
licenses to houses in the vicinity of theatrrs,
&c. It was decided that a deputation should
again wait upon the Commissioner to inform
him of their views regarding the matter.

articles.title: Nov. 16, 1872
articles.text:
Nov. 16, 1872

_
NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF

MINERS.

CONPEIIitIiCE AT DI.II9IAM.
The annual Conference of the Miners' National
Association commenced on Monday in the Town
hall, Durham. The Association in question has
been in existence since 1863, and must not be
confounded with the: kindred body—the Amalga-
mated Association of Miners of Great Britain,
fcunded three or four years ago; the Association
under notice devoting itself especially to the for.
warding of all Parliamentary business connected
with the mining interest. The business of the
Conference commenced at three o'clock. Mr.
Alex. M'Donald, the chairman of the association,
took his place, and the proceedings commenced.
The secretary, Mr. Burt, Northumberland, then
read over the names of the delegates present, as
-follows :—Bouth Yorkshire, 12,000 financial mem-
bers; West Yorkshire, 8,000; Durham, 35,000
Northumberland, 13,000; Ashton, 2,000; Bristol,
510; Fifeshire and Clackmannan, 4,491 ; Mid and
East Lothian, 2,050; Stirling and Linlithgow,
2,000; Marybill, 1,500; Larkhall, 1,150; High
Blantyre, 170; Cleveland Ironstone Mines, 5,000.
Total number of financial members represented,
86,871 ; number of delegates present, 26.
The President traced the origin of their union'
from the time of the passing of the Mines Regula-
tion Bill in 1855, a measure which created uni-
versal dissatisfaction amongst the working miners
of the kingdom, and led to the formation of an
Association amongst that community in South
Yorkshire. From that body sprang, in 1863,
the National Association, its objects being to
obtain legislative action for the amelioration of the
condition of the working miners of the kingdom.
Since the formation of the Association it had been
exposed to many trials to which other kindred
combinations luld succumbed, but through which
they bad successfully ridden, and they had
gathered strength until at that meeting they had
represented 86,871 members—a feature of organi-
zation complete in its individual parts, and second
to none in the civilized world amongst working
men. (Cheers.),,He then referred to the severance
of a portion of their members, who thought they
should take charge of every district; but he held
that local branches were the best to look after
questions affecting themselves only, and they
were the best to counsel the proper steps to be
taken. On this question a federation had sepa-
rated am the parent body. They were, however,
working for the same principles as this Associe.-
tion, and were also working heartily with them,
being only divided in the, manner he had
noted. He then proceeded to review the
Work of the Association since its formation,
and, in the first place, referred to the old relations
of master and servant, by which the former could
only be proceeded against by civil process when
infringing a contract, whereas the servant was
dealt with criminally, and could be sent to prison
• for three months' hard labour if convicted of that
offence: Towards putting the proceedings against
either muter or servant on a civil law footing,
that Association had taken a leading part. He
next referred tp the fact that but a short time ago
Trades Unions had been pointed to as combinations
of associations, or people banded together to up-
set all law and order. That Assoeiation had' by
its action seoured the Government Commission on
the subject, the inquiry of which had conclusively
proved they were nothing like what they had
been represented to be, and the result of which
was to put Trades Unions on the footing of a
private banking association. He next referred to
the Mines Regulation Bill, which ho believed
would be a boon to working miners if carried out
to the letter, and in its spirit. It rested, however,
with the workmen themselves to see that this was
done, and he hoped that meeting, before it
separated, would counsel some measures with that
object. He next referred to the question of
wages, for the weekly payment of which ho hoped
the Governnaent would bring in a Bill next
session. The next question was that of com-
pensation for injury sustained by workmen in
following their calling, and the speaker intimated
that Mr. Fortescue had, on behalf of the Govern-
ment, promised to bring in a Bill on this subject
during next session, so that he hoped in cases of
accident the existing law would be very materially
altered. He next referred to the uncertain tenure
on which a colliery workman holds his dwelling,
and having referred to a number of evictions which
have within the last few years been made in the
district about Durham, he hoped that when the
Attorney-General buckled on his armour to amelio-
rate the condition of the agricultural labourer, so
that he could not be turned out to find his resting
place on the hill side, whenever he had a difficulty
with his master, that impel:tent member of the
Goyernment would also do something to alter the

existing tenure on which the miner held. kis dwell-
ing, 'which was much akin to that of the agricultural
labourer. In conclusion, he referred to the amicable
feeling existing in Durham, Northumberland, and
Yorkshire, where the representatives of the men
frequently meet the employers for the settlement of
disputes; but he pointed out that while the men
of these counties could combine as they had done,
they might as easily by co•operation become em-
ployers and own mines themselves. This subject
he recommended to the consideration of miners,
and, in resuming his seat, he hoped prosperity and
peace would attend the mining interest.
A vote of thanks to the President having been
given, the meeting adjourned until the next
morning.

TUESDAY.

The business was resumed this morning in the
Town-hall, Durham, Mr. A. M'Dmuild, presiding.
The number of delegates was increased by the
presence of a representative from Warwickshire,
who attended as delegate from 1,200 financial
members.
The first business was the reception of the
report as to the state of affairs in the various
districts represented in each section. There was
stated to be a most satisfactory increase of financial
•members compared with those enrolled 12 months
ago, while the funds in hand were also satisfactory.
The delegate from East and Mid Lothian spoke to
the men of a colliery being discharged on the spot
by their employer, Mr. Moore, who having written
to the other colliery owners of the county re-
questing them not to employ his men, then sum-
moned the latter before the magistrates for not
leaving his houses, and they were found guilty on
. Saturday last. This conduct he stamped as un-

mitigate.d tyranny.
At the close of the delivery of the reports it
was unanimously agreed that the various reports
were deemed satisfactory.

The Chairman then delivered the report of the
Parliamentary Committee, and in doing so entered
into a long statement of the action taken by the
Parliamentary Committee and the difficulties they
encountered in passing the Mines Regulation Bill.
He expreised his greatest confidence in the good
that would be secured for the mining community
by the working of that measure, and ho explained,
in answer to regrets that had been expressed,
that educational clauses had not been embodied in
the Bill, because the Government were legislating
specially on that question.
It was then moved by Mr. Grieves, Northum-
berland, seconded by Mr. King, Cleveland—
That a vote of thanks be tendered to the
Parliamentary Committee, and that this Con-
ference pledges itself to use its whole powers to
enforce the provisions of the Mines Regulation
Bill in all parts of the country.

The meeting then, proceeded to consider the
payment of wages question, and various delegates
having spoken in favour of the weekly payments,
it was unanimously agreed, on the motion of Mr.
Wilson, of Larkhill, seconded by Mr. Shepherd,
of Cleveland— _

-- -
That the Government be urged at the next
Session of Parliament to introduce in its original
form the Payment of Wags Bill, providing
weekly payments without any deductions.

The next item on the programme was compensa-
tion for loss of life in the mines, and on this
question the Conference was unanimous in the
opinion that the owners should be liable to pay
compensation to relatives df men killed by the
ignorance or negligence of their representatives,
and a resolution was moved by Mr. Crawford, of
Durham, seconded by Mr. Jacobs, of Bristol—
That the Government be urged to introduce a
Bill which will render the obtaining of compensa-
tion in cases of loss of life a matter of less
difficulty tha,n at present.

The meeting then, after a short discussion,
adopted a resolution, moved by Mr. Moulson, of
Yorkshire, and seconded by Mr. Booth, of Ashton,
ailing upon the Government to amend or abolish
the Criminal Law Amendment Act as early as
possible in the next Session of Parliament.
It was then agreed to reform the Parliamentary
Committee for the transaction of the legislative
business affecting the mining affairs during the
next Session of Parliament. Mr. Alexander
3WDonald, Mr. John Normanstlll, Mr. Thomas
Burt, and Mr. John Dixon were appointed to
form the committee, with power to add to their
number.

The Chairman drew attention to the late ex-
plosion of gas at Morley Colliery, by which 33
lives were lost, and as it was clear to him that
the accident was the result of negligence on the
part of those in charge of the mines, he thought
it wc.i.s due to the relatives of the deceased that
some steps should he taken to obtain compensation
for them.

After till explanation from Mr. Dixon, of South
Yorkshire,

It was proposed by Mr. Grieves, of Northumber-
land, and seconded by Mr. Gibson, of Yorkshire— ,
That it be left with the Parliamentary Committee
to take such steps as they may deem necessary in
the case of the Morley explosion, either in the
way of obtaining compensation or of punishing
the manager.

WEDNESDAY.

The business of the Conference was resumed
this morning in the Town Hall, Durham; Mr.

Alexander 311Tonald presiding.

The first business of the assembly was the con-
sideration .of certain unsatisfactory features in the
reports of some of the districts. The first taken
was the refusal of Messrs. Hope and Pearson, of
the Normanton Collieries, in West Yorkshire, to
allow check weighmen belonging to the Union to
officiate on the pit heap. On this question it was
agreed that the president and officers of the asso-
ciation should place themselves in communication
with the owners of the colliery, in order to bring
about a better understanding between employers
and employed. The Conference .also approved
the manner in which the workmen at the collieries
in question had conducted themselves under the
trying circumstances alluded to, and thought it
would be wanting in its duty if it did not recom-
mend every district connected with it to come for-
ward and give its vote in favour of that association
rendering every requirecrpeouniary and moral sup-
port to the West Yorkshire_miners until they can
establish their rights.

The next feature in the reports was the com-
plaints of the Cleveland ironstOne miners, whose
delegates described in vivid terms the sufferings
of the men from bad ventilation.
Mr. Foreman, of Durham, pronounced the state
of the Cleveland district to be barbarous. It was
agreed that the Parliamentary Committee should
lay the matter before the Home Secretary, a de-
putation of the Cleveland men to be present on
that occasion to furnish any information required.
It was also agreed that Mr. Foreman, president of
the Durham Union, ancl'Mr. Grieves, president of
that of Northumberland, should visit the Cleve-
land mines if the consent of the owner could be ob-
tained, in order, if possible, to examine the extent
of the grievances complained of by the delegates
from that district.

• The case of the men belonging to the Ponstone
Colliery, in East Lothian, was next taken into
consideration, and it was stated that on the
..men
going to their employers to complain of bad
ventilation in the pit they had all been dischmed ;
that on applying at the other collieries for
employment they bad been told in two or
three instances that their employers had

written to request that none of them should be

employed. Some of the men had also been served
with summonses for not quitting their houses, and
on Saturday last the Sheriff of the district decided
against them after hearing the statements of the
delegates.
A resolution was adopted condemning the con-
duct of the owners in preventing the men from
finding employment and homes, and it was agreed
that the whole matter be placed in the hands of
the Parliamentary Committee for representation to.
the Home Secretary.
It was then agreed that the president, Mr.
M'Donald, and Mr. William Crawford, of Dur-
ham, should represent the association at the Trades'
Union Congress, which will be held on the Bth of
January next.
It was also agreed to issue among the members a
monthly circular showing the state of wages in the
various districts, and embodying other important
matters connected with the mining interest.
It was then agreed to present an illuminated
address to each of the gentlemen who aided the
miners in Parliament in getting the Mines'
Regulation Bill made law.

articles.title: EAST AND WEST INDIA DOCK
articles.text:
THE EAST AND WEST INDIA DOCK

LABOURERS.

A crowded meeting of men employed in the East
and West India,Docks, Poplar, was held on Monday
evening, at the Eastern-hall, Litnehouse ; Mr. T.
C. Pato occupied the chair. The object of the
meeting, as stated in the announcement, was to
take into consideration the late reduction of the
labourers' wages. The chairman, in opening the
meeting, stated that when he consented to act as
chairman he did so with a full sense of the reason-
ableness of the request the dock labeurers were
about to make. if he understood the question
rightly, the, agitation during the past summer
caused the dock authorities to raise the labourers'
wages to 6i. per hour, and the ordinary hours of
working were from 8 o'clock until 4. By this
system the man who could ensure constant cm-
ployment earned a week. The grievance under
which the men now complain is, that the Customs
authorities open the gates at nine instead of eight

3 ,

in tho morning; the consequence is, the labourer,
at a season when he is likely to require most, finds
himself earning 6d. per day less.
Mr. Ellwood proposed, and Mr. O'Brien se-
conded

That a memorial be addressed to the Lords of
the Treasury, praying that the Customs authorities
be authorized to have the bonded and other de-
partments open eight. hours per day all the year
*round.

The chairman having invited any one in the
meeting to speak upon the question, the resolution
was put atid carried unanimously, as was the
following, moved by Mr. Brown, and seconded
by Mr. Solloway :
That Colonel Duplat Taylor be appealed to to
continue the 3s. 4d. for. the seven hours' work
until the question is settled with her Majesty's
Treasury. _ _

A hearty vote of thanks having been accorded
,o the chairman, the meeting dissolved.

Mr. Rupert Kettle has given his decision with

Board of Arbitration in the north. The decision

"Great Western Hotel, London, Nov. 9,
With reference reference to cases submitted to me by the

factured Iron Trade of the North of England, the
following resolutions have been adopted:— After
full investigation of the claims of sundry classes
of men employed in and about the mills and

Company, it is resolved that the claimants are

Ironworks, Fence Houses.—Whereas at these
mills and-forges the wages of the classes of work-
men now making a claim for n rise have heretofore

employers and workmen, and not upon the basis

articles.title: TUE STAPPORDSHLRE POTTERS.
articles.text:
TUE STAPPORDSHLRE POTTERS.

To the great relief of the entire district, the
operative potters of Staffordshire have withdrawn
their demand for payment on "good from hand,"
instead of "good from oven." Had the demand
been persisted in, a general lock-out woulehave
been made at the oil of the present week, in
which ease from 2.5,000 to 36,000 persons would
have been deprived of employment. The men
wore strengthened in their demand by the faet
that the leading house of Minton and Co. had
consented to pay on "good from hand," but,
with this exception, the whole of the manufacturers
were perfoptly unanimous in their determining to
resist to the last extremity the radical change in
the customs of the trade which would have been
involved in acceding to the demand mentioned.
The annual hiring this Martinmas is, apart front
this dispute, proceeding less satisfactorily than
usual; but both sides are prepared to submit all
minor disputes to the decision of the local Board
of Arbitration.

articles.title: TRONFOUNDERS OF ENGLAND,
articles.text:
TRONFOUNDERS OF ENGLAND,

IRELAND, AND WALES.

The following appears in the 220th Monthly
report:—

Brother Members,—ln taking a casual glanee at
the column for the state of trade, as well " 1116
numbers on the donative benefit, it will be per.

eeived that there is a alight movement downwards,
as far as trade is concerned; further, it will be
seen that there is an increase on that fund of 56.
True, the increase is not a great one, but a straw
will show which way the stream flows; and it is
a very wise arrangement that it should be so, for
it very often enables us to prepare for any emer-
gency that may cross out path. There is no doubt
at all that there is plenty of trade in the country
still, in orders not yet completed; and.the signs of
a lull or quietness arise to a great extent from the

rel uctance evident on the part of employers in our
trade not to take in fresh orders until the raw
material—coal and iron—come down to their
legitimate level. No doubt that will be the case
before long; and from the most reliable resources,
we have information that though there may be a
slight slackness during the winter months, there
can be little doubt that we shall have, in spring, a
good trade. There is not much to create alarm at

present; our men are well employed, wages are
tolerably
,good, and we have the benefit of the
short-time movement to fall back upon. No doubt,
If there should be anything like a marked reaction
in the state of trade, the question of the number of
hours will be the first thing considered by the em-

ployers ; it will therefore be necessary for us to ho

_ -
watchful, and guard the boon of short hours with
a very vigilant eye, as we are satisfied, in our own
minds, there has been nothing granted to the work-
man during the present century that is so well
calculated to amend his position as the lessening
his hours of labour—it not only gives him time to
recreate his physical energies, but it also, if
properly used, enables him to cultivate his mind;
and when the two peoperties of mind and matter
are rightly and properly exercised, we may be
assured that the toiler for bread will have a better
chance of mending his position; and we may fur-
ther say, t} at it is only by a proper use of these
two faculties—combined with economy of those
things—we real ze by their use that we shall be
able to retain the / dvantages we at present enjoy.
Ours is not an aggro sive policy; but Wo shall be
compelled, if needs be, to struggle hard to retain
what little of labours' result we at present receive,
and we were never in a better condition, finan-
cially, than we are at present, for doing so,—our
cash in hand at the end of last month being
£35,849. DANIEL GUILE.

200, New Kent-road, London, S.E.,
November Bth, 1872.

articles.title: WEAVERS' STRIKE AT
articles.text:
THE WEAVERS' STRIKE AT

BARNSLEY.

On Wednesday a meeting of the power-loom linen
manufacturers of Barnsley was held in the Tem-
peranee Hall, to decide on the steps to be taken
with regard to the strike at Messrs. Richardson,
Tee, and Co.'s for an advance of 1.5 per cent. of
wages, and which the men stated would be de-
manded from all the other employers. The
weavers were invited to attend, and there was a
strong muster of them present. Amongst the
firms represented were those of Richarcison, Tee,
and Co., Carter Brothers, Pigott and Sons,
Spencer and Co., Scales, Outwin, and Jackson,
Cantor, Whaloy, and Co., Sykes, TWIN -ell, and
Co.

_
Alderman Carter occupied the chair, and in in-
thQ Juines,a4id the quemixt ttaly were

articles.title: TITE BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
TITE BEE-HIVE.

called upon to discuss was one that not only
*affected the firm of Messrs. Richardson and Co.,
but that of every other firm in the town, for the
men had very fairly stated that the advance of 15
per cent. would be required from all the manu.
facturerers if conceded by the firm struck against.
Mr. Broughton (for the workmen) said the men
had, had a meeting amongst themselves, and had
agreed to adhere to the terms as stated at the
last conference—that work could only be resumed
on the advance being granted.
Mr. Chappell (another working man) said the
men asked for an advance of 16 per cent., and he
should like to know what offer the masters had
to make.

The Chairman said the masters could make no
advance whatever. The manufacturers did not
refuse the demand of the men because it was
made, but because they were burdened by a weight
of competition which the workpeople were un-
aware of, that they could not do so. He hoped the
weavers of Barnsley would see it to be their
interest to aid the manufacturers in preventing the
trade leaving the town.
The proceedings then terminated.

While we do not under-estimate the difficulties
of reform, we still think that with careful pffort
and united action it would be comparatively easy
to make our trade rank one of the best paid in
London. The fact that in some few shops the
men are fairly paid is sufficient proof that all
could be so, and would be so,if the men exhibited,
by a strong society, a universal determination to
demand, as the price of their labour, a fair and
reasonable wage.
As a programme for the future we can at pre-
sent only submit two or three urgently needed
reforms, lat. The revision of the present price-
book, so that all kinds of work may be fairly paid
for. 2nd. Fixing a minimum rate of wages per
hour, so that no man shall work, as at present,
for 4d. or 4id. 3rd. Destroying the obnoxious
practice by which the piecemaster is allowed to
step between the employers and men, and with-
out labour, and for his personal benefit, Jdeduct
from 25 to 60 per cent. of the legitimate earnings
of the men.

We would advise that at least the whole of the
winter should be devoted to the work of organiza-
tion, and that no effort should be made until the
majority of the workmen are united for the
struggle. The lamentable failures recently made
by some trades is a warning to us not to act
until we can rely upon each other, and also
possess sufficient funds to carry us through the
work.

Our policy must be one of moderation and con-
ciliation. The waste of time and capital, the
miseries and privations that a strike inevitably
entails upon all, are arguments sufficiently power.
ful in themselves to make us use every legitimate
means to avoid the employment of that weapon to
gain our ends; and we are thankful that the policy
of trades unions is now in favour of employing
arbitration to settle trade disputes.
We appeal to all to join and aid us, confident
that the powerful forces of right and justice are
on our side, and that, if we are guided by reason
and moderation, we shall be able to win for our
trade a fair position among other industries, and
for ourselves a better lot in life.
MAGEE PRATT, Gen. Sec.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
THE BIRMINGHAM BUILDING
TRADES.

A partial lock-out occurred in the building
trade on Monday. Last week the Builders' Asso-
ciation issued notices to the effect that the work-
ing hours for all branches, both in workshops and
out of doors, would be from seven a.m. to five
p.m. on and after Monday, Nov. 11, till geh.
18, 1873. This, the men say, is contrary to the
rules as decided by Mr. Rupert Kettle, and they
accordingly issued a counter notice that the short
time would not commence till Wednesday.

On Monday ' morning last, regardless of the
notices issued by the employers, the men went to
the works at the usual time, six o'clock, but at
three firms—Mr. Hardwick, Messrs. Cresswell and
Sons, and Mr. Williams—the doors were found
to be locked. The men thereupon left the pre-
mises.

On Tuesday afternoon a conference of the
employers and a deputation of the men was held
,at the Woolpack Hotel, Moor-street. Captain
Briggs occupied the chair. There was considerable
discussion, in which the men asserted that they
had accurately interpreted the rule, and the
masters maintained an opposite view, and ultimately
it was resolved that Mr. Rupert Kettle should be
asked to state the correct signification of the dis-
puted rule. Mr. Bloore was selected as the repre-
sentative of the employers, and Messrs. Laughton
and Waldron as those of the men, and it was re-
solved that these three men should proceed to
Wolverhampton and lay the matter before Mr.
Kettle, asking him to givb his decision as quickly
as possible. Meanwhile the men resume work
upon the old conditions.
Mr. Hardwick declared that be should require
some explanation from his men before he permitted
them to recommence work in his premises, as they
bad violated one of the rules by striking work
instead of working under protest and submitting
the matter to arbitration.

articles.title: BRISTOL CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE BRISTOL CARPENTERS.

It will be remembered that the last Aispute
between the employers and the operative carpen-
ters and joiners in Bristol was settlekby arbitra-
tion, Mr. Lewis Fry being the umpire—a gentle-
man of the operatives' delegates own proposing.
Mr. Fry having heard all that both aides had to
,say, decided that the offer made by the employers
was fair and reasonable, and gave his award
accordingly. For some time, ho vever, it has
been pretty well known that this decision was far
from satisfactory to the operatives, and a meeting
of the several bodies has been lately held to de-
termine what stops should be taken to gain what
was originally asked for, in other words to refuse
to abide by Mr. Fry's award. The meeting was
to a certain extent a closed one, for neither the
names of any of the speakers nor the name of the
chairman has transpired. No doubt they will
work in accordance with the umpire's ruling till
the prescribed time, but it is more than probable
the employers will ere long receive another in-
timation that an alteration in the present rate of
pay will be pxpeeted. The labourers of Bristol
and the neighbourhood have also called a mass
meeting for the purpose of organizing a union.

articles.title: Nov. 16, 1872.
articles.text:
Nov. 16, 1872.

ELECTORAL REFORM.

A conference, convened by the Electoral Reform
Association, was held at noon on Tuesday, in one
of the smaller rooms of St. James's Hall, to hear
several papers read upon various subjects interest-
ing to Reformers. Mr. Joseph Chamberlain,
Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Edu-
cation League presided, and among those present
were Sir Charles Dilke, Mr. D. Pratt, Mr. Lloyd
,Jones, Mr. George Potter, Mr. Howell, Mr. R. M.
Latham, Mr. Faceypr. D. Cameron, of Glasgow;
Mr. Hall, of Shoreham ; Mr. Henry Brooks; Mr.
Joseph Arch, President of the Labciurers' Union;
Mr. Taylor, of Peterborough; Mr. Biggs, formerly
M.P. for Newport; Mr. Stephen Winkwortb, of
Bolton; Mr. Collins and Mr. Hallam, of Man-
chester; Mr. D uignon, of Walsall; Captain Maxse,
R.N.", Mr. J. S. Wright, Chairman of the Birming-
ham Liberal Association; Mr. Cooper, of Nor-
wich; Mr. Shipton, Mr. J. 0. Cox, of Belper ; Mr.
E. Jenkins, Mr. Gates, Lincoln, Eco. About 120
persons were present, and besides the metropolitan
boroughs, the following towns and societies were
said to be represented :—Croydon, Southampton,
Shoreham, Portsmouth, Brighton, Birmingham,
Derby, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Paisley, Dundee,
Aberdeen, Newcastle,:Manchester, Bolton, Walsall,
Bristol, Bath, Colchester, Belper, Plaistow, Wey-
mouth, Oxford, Coventry, Leicester, Liverpool,
Warrington, Leeds, Peterborough, Norwich,
Northampton, Cambridge, King's -Lynn, North
Shields, Eaton and Normanby, Belfist, West-
bromwich, Lincoln, Labour Representation League,
10 Trade (Londop) Societies, the National Educa-
tion League, the Westminster Working Men's
Liberal Association, the Soothill Upper Liberal
Association, Greenwich Advanced Liberal Asso-
ciation, Walsall R adical Reformers, Newcastle
Liberal Association, and the National Reform
Union.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said,
representing as he did, on that question at least,
the great bulk of the Liberals in the three counties
of Warwick, Worcester, and Stafford, he could
assert that Liberal feeling in those counties wets
unanimously in favour of the equalization of the
borough and the county franchise. He did not
believe any remedy was to be found for the suffer-
ings of agricultural labourers save in the power
which the possession of a vote would offer.
(Cheers.) The great constituencies were, he
thought, universally in favour of a redistribution
of seats. While Birmingham, with a population
of 343,000, returned three members, 13 othe
towns, with an aggregate population of 313,000,
returned 20. Evesham had relatively 23 times,
and Lichfield 15 times, the voting power of Bir-
mingham. The Association heartily protested
against any system which would perpetuate that
unmitigated nuisance the representation of minori-
ties. (Cheers.)
The reading of papers on different subjects then
commenced.

Mr. J. A. Has lam, of Bolton, read the first paper.
"On Redistribution as affecting Lancashire."
The population of Lancashire has, he said in-
creased at double the natural rate, while it had
only half the number of members that it was
entitled to.

Mr. Briggs, formerly M.P. for Newport, Isle of
Wight, followed with another paper on the same
subject. Taking the population of the British
Isles, in accordance with the last census, at
32,000,000, it followed that 658 members of the
House of Commons gave one member for about
every 50,000. The metropolis was the least-
represented portion of the kingdom. Marylebone,
containing a population of 477,000, returned two
members, and should proportionately return nine;
Finsbury, having a population of 443,000, returned
two, and should return eight; Hackney, having
a population of 362,000, returned two, and should
return seven; the City of London, having a
population of 74,000, returned four, and should
return only one. Liverpool, with a population of
493,000, returned three members, and should
return nine; Manchester, with a population of
383,000, returned three, and should return seven.
To sum up the whole, the metropolis, with its
population of 3,008,000, returned 22 members,
and should return 55; 17 large provincial towns,
with a population of 3,269,000, returned 37
members, and should return 65; while 60 small
boroughs, with an aggregate population of only
417,000, returned GO, and should return only eight.
The great provincial towns had always wished to
look to London for guidance in that respect, but
bad never found it.

Mr. D. Cameron, of Glasgow, read a paper
"On Redistribution as affecting. Scotland," show-
ing that in many of the Fimall coustitwnoies the
votes represent a power iliteen times 4S' as
as
that represented by votes in Glasgow.

articles.title: Nov. 16, 1872.
articles.text:
Nov. 16, 1872.

the object of which was to show that a proper re-
gard for the amount of population and of income
tax would tend to transfer a large part of the pre-
sent representation from small agricultural
boroughs in the south and west of England to
London and other large towns. He contended
that the wisest course the Association could adopt
was to go for uniformity in the borough and county
suffrage.
Mr. J. C. Cox, of Belper, read a paper " On
Redistribution generally," in the course of which
a warm tribute, heartily responded to by the Con-
ference, was paid to Mr. Arch as the founder ol a
great movement for the benefit of the agricultural
community.
A discussion on the subject of these papers then
took place.
Mr. J. S. Wright, Birmingham, moved the fol-
lowing resolution :

That such a readjustment of constituencies
should be effected as would make the power of the
elector in any one constituency equal to the power
of the elector in any other.

Captain Maas° having seconded the resolu-
tion—
- •

Mr. George Potter, who supported the resolution,
deprecated lethargy on this question in the next
Session of Parliament, and urged that Mr. Glad-
stone should then re-unite the Liberal party by
bringing forward a great scheme of electoral re-
distribution. It was also necessary that industry
should be recognized, and the working classes
should no longer be contented to play second fiddle
to the middle classes. A proper lodger franchise
and a franchise for the agricultural labourer were
absolutely essential.
Mr. E. Jenkins said the Conference ought to
recognize the fact that a redistribution of seats
was not a party question, but an attempt to remedy
imperfection in the relations between population
and representation. He advocated the system of
equal electoral districts, where you would have
counter influences arrayed against and balancing
each other; and he thought that if the Govern-
ment meant V bring forward any such reforms
they ought not to keep their proposals lockel up,
but to avow them, and try to educate the people
up to them.
Mr. G. Howell advocated proportional representa -
tion according to population—not equal geographi-
eel districts. To break up Manchester and
Birmingham, for instance, into wards would be to
multiply mediocrity. What was wanted was a
system which would prevent jerrymandering, and
give us diversified representation.
Mr. Lloyd Jones pointed out the necessity of
immediate action. They were getting out of the
old rotten borough system, and were now in a
position to avail themselves of experience and
ability.
Mr. Mottershead, speaking as an old Chartist,
complained of the mediocre character of the zepre-
sentation and of the influence which was exercised
by mere money. He wished to see every phase of
opinion represented in Parliament.
Mr. Jesse Collins (Birmingham) wished to see
the abuses :of class legislation removed. He pro-
tested against any system of preferential voting.
Mr. Henry Brookes thou proceeded to read n
paper " On the Right of Labour to the Fran-
chise." The number of :agricultural labourers in
the country was about 800,000, but they were de-
barred from exorcising the constitutional rights of
Englishmen. The question was whether they
ever had a right to deprive the labourers of their
electoral rights. They !did not ask for the fran-
chise for the labours as a privilege, but as a right
which they were entitled to demand, and which
no one had a right to withhold.
Mr. W. Hall, of Shoreham, read an elaborate
piper "On Registration."
Mr. Catt4ll, of Birmingham, having seconded
the -resolution; and Mr. George Shipton and other
gentlemen having spoken,
Mr. Elthorne expressed dcubts whether the
agricultural labourers, as a body, were sufficiently
educated to exercise the franchise.

111 r. joseph Arch, in reply, said he stood there
as an agricultural labourer, and a representative of
the claims of men. He was sorry anyone should
have spoken of the inefficiency of his brethren.
He, did not know whether he referred to their
good sense or their good cottages, but he wanted
to know if the agricultural labourer lived in bad
cottages, whose fault it was. As a class of men
they were not so intelligent as they ought to be,
but whose fault was it P With regard to the
assertion that landowners would control their
votes, he did not see how that could follow now
that voters had got the ballot. He thought, if
'the agricultural labourer had the franchise, his
bad cottage would soon be turned into a good one,
and his education and general condition, as well as
his fitness to exercise the franchise, would soon be
greatly improved,

Mr. A. Clayden and Mr. C. Murray addressed
the meeting, the latter gentleman expressing the
opinion that the movement was not on a basis of
sufficient breadth.

Sir C. Mike, M.P., in reply, said that since
Chartist times there had been no movement claim -
ing equal electoral districts. Since that time
there had been no attempt to do more than to re-
distribute a dozen or so of seats. It must be
remembered that Government would not move in
the matter without immense pressure from outside.
There were only 96 members in the House who se
seats would not be affected by such a movement,
and 16 of those were Tories, leaving only 80 who
would be in favour of the movement. These
facts showed the meeting that the association
would have enough to do.

Mr. Spencer, of the Marylebone Reform Associa-
tion, spoke on the importance of an improved re-
gistration system, and urged the necessity of
amendment, especially to prevent the improper
disqualification of ledgers.
Mr. George Potter, by the permission of the
chairman, moved a resolution—
Declaring that any measure to secure a redis-
tribution of seats and electoral reform would be
incomplete and undeserving of the support of
working men if it did not rectify the great injus-
tice now inflicted on lodgers in large towns, and
secure a good Registration Bill.
The resolution having been seconded, a discussion
ensued, and it was adopted unanimously.
Mr. R. Marsden Latham, Chairman of the
Labour Representation League, read a paper
"On Election Expenses," which he said was a
vital question to working men, the present system
involving their exclusion from the House of Com-
mons. Mr. Henry James and Mr. Vernon Har-
court after the course they had pursued on that
question could not be regarded as friends of the
working classes.
On the motion of Mr. Kennedy the following
resolution was adopted :
That the Chairman be asked to sign a petition
to the House of Commons in favour of the reforms
sanctioned by ,resolution this day ; that a Com-
mittee, composed of delegates from country asso-
ciations and of the existing Executive Committee
of the Electoral Refs= Association, meet imme-
diately to elect a treasurer and receive subscrip-
tions; and that an early application be made to
Mr. Gladstone to receive a deputation in support of
the views advocated by the association.
The Chairman announced two subscriptions of
£l,OOO each per annum, conditional on the sum
of £30,000 being raised. Some other sums were
promised.
Mr. Walton, Brecon, moved a resolution for the
prevention of systematic canvassing, and provid-
ing that provision should be made for its suppres-
sion, and that it should be made a misdemeanour,
punishable with imprisonment. Carried._

On the motion of Mr. Cooper, Norwich, a re-
solution was passed declaring that no electoral
system would be satisfactory which did not pro..
vent paid canvassing, relieve the candidates from
the official expense, and extend the hours of poll-
ing to 8 o'clock.
The proceedings terminated at half-past five
with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

articles.title: EVENING MEETING.
articles.text:
THE EVENING MEETING.

In the evening a public) meeting was held in
St. James's Hull, when the chair was taken by Sir
C. Dilke, who was accompanied by Lady Dilke,
and supported by a number of prominent metro-
politan and provincial Liberals.
The Chairman explained the results of the con-
ference Earl road letters of apology from Mr. Peter
Taylor, M.P., Mr. Dixon, M.P., Mr. Carter, M.P
and Mr. Odger.

The chairman (in opening the proceedings) ob-
served that they were met that night to introduce
" principle " into the county franchise and into
distribution of seats, viz., the principle of equality
of franchise and equality of political power. He
believed that the time was ripe for these reforms.
In regard to the redistribution of political powert
Mr. Bright had urged it with all the powers of his
eloquence in 1859.1860, before he became a mem-
ber of the Government ; yet no step had been made
in that direction. The anomalies of the present
system were glaring : and it was impossible to find
any argument why an elector of Marylebone
should only possess 1-120th or 1-240th of the
electoral powsr possessed by an elector of Port-
arliugton. (Cheers.) Now that was one of the
strongest cases that be could put. But taking
them haphazard, just as they came, the following
places stood consecutively on the list of Englieh
and Scotch boroughs, leaving out the Irish, which
were worse still, but which might be viewed as
standing by themselves—Eye, Falkirk, Finsbury,
Flint, and Frome. Nov', Eye, Falkirk, Flint, and
Frome had together about 6,000 voters, but they
returned twice as many members as Finsbury
with its 36,000 electors. A. little further on in the
list they had the following
towns coming together

—Liverpool, London, Ludlow, and Lymington.
Ludlow had 50,000 and London 20,000—that was
70,000 between those two latter, or an average of
10,000 voters to one member; while in Ludlow and
Lymington there were 700 voters to a member.
Taking London all through, tho City and metro-
politan districts together, there were about
300,000 voters, without counting the people who
lived in Croydon, and Battersea, and the extreme
north-east of London, who went unheard. But
those 300,000 voters, representing between three
and four millions of people, had but 22 members
amongst them. The whole of the Irish boroughs
had but 60,000 voters, but they had 37 members,
although they had only one-sixth as many
voters as there were in London, which
returned only twenty-two. Birmingham, Man-
chester, Liverpool, and Glasgow had each of them
more voters than there were in the whole of the
Irish boroughs put together, and each of them had
but three members instead of 37. There were
a hundred members of the house who eat for about
1,080,000 voters. There were another hundred
members who sat for about the odd 80,000 voters.
He believed that in many respects the people were
as badly off now as they were before the Reform
Act of 1832; the influence was felt almost as
much now as then, the list of boroughs was almost
endless in which the politics of the people were of
no avail against the holders of landed property in
the neighbourhood, and it was notorious that there
were at least 100 members of the House of Com-
mons who were the direct nominees of peers, in spite
of the law against the interference of members of
the Upper Chamber in elections. (Hear.) In conclu-
ding he observed that if there were any cause that
could justify an agitation it was surely that which
had brought this meeting together. (Cheers.) Ho
hoped he should not be liable to be fined £6 for
saying that (a laugh and cheers.) But was it not
monstrous that the people of London should be
denied the opportunity of expressing such an
opinion unless they paid for a hall in which to
hold their meetings? He did not always approve
of what was said in Hydo Park, but whether the
words were foolish or wise, it was clearly right
and better that they should be expressed than that
they shoulil be suppressed. (Cheers,)
Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, of Birmingham,
moved the first resolution as follows :

That such a re-adjustment of constituencies
should be effected as would make the power of
the elector in any one constituency equal to the,
power of the elector in any other.
He based his ease on the fact that only one-
third of the adult male population had votes; that
one-fifth of that ono-third returned half the exist-
ing House of Commons; and that Birmingham,
with 350,000 inhabitants, was balanced by Eve-
sham, Lichfield, and Droitwich with 22,000. The
House of Commons, though representing such
interests as that of banking, railways, the parsons,
and even the publicans, failed to represent the
interests of the working classes.

Mr. J. B. Torr, Q.C., of Manchester, seconded
the resolution, contending that household suffrage
was the thin end of the wedge, that the old unit
was class and the new one was men and it was
known now what there was to distribute, and they
must come to manhood suffrage.
The resolution was then put to the meeting, and
carried unanimously with loud cheers.
Mr. J. Arch, the president of the agricultural
labourers' movement, moved the second resolution,
which was:—

That it is desirable to assimilate the county and
borough franchise, whatever basis of qualification
may be adopted.
Ile commented on the condition of the county
franchise, claiming manhood suffrage, and credit
for pointing out the position of a class whose
condition was a danger to the country. Many
well-meaning gentlemen felt timid at
.the idea of
the agricultural labourers having representative
power, but he could only pity their nervous
debility. The labourers in ther movement had
• shown they were not very dangerous, for they had
been remarkably law-aUiding, consistent, and fair.
Conversations he had had with gentlemen in
London satisfied him that they were not aware
how the agricultural labourers were serfed. Ire
was, however, acquainted with his own class, who
as a body, were at starvation point. As regards
the alleged disqualification of the labourer for the
franchise, on• account of his political ignorance,
he said that it was like advising a boy not to go
into the water until he had learned how to swim.
The franchise would supply the means of political
education.

Sir John Bennett seconded the resolution, advo-
cating the cause of the emancipation of the
agricultural labourers as the only means of
elevating and improving their present deplorable
condition, which he compared with the position of
men whom he had assisted to the Western States
of America..

Mr. E. Jenkins supported the resolution, ex-
pressing the opinion that nothing could be more
just, proper, and reasonable than the demand of
the agricultural labourer for the franchise. He
repudiated the existence of any reason for the dif-
ference between the urban and county franchise,
and declared that the agricultural labourer was a
sharper person than people gave him credit for,
his only disability being the feeling that the nobler
and better things of which he was capable had no
outlet, from the lack of political representation.
Political representation was the only means of
giving them the political education they required;
and, therefore, he was in favour of the resolution—
assimilation of the county and borough franchise
being, in his opinion, precedent to redistribution
of seats.
The resolution was carried unanimously.

Mr. Shipton then moved a resolution, which the
Chairman explained did not emanate from the

committee, viz.,

That it would be unwise for this meeting to dis-
solve without expressing its firm conviction that
any reform in our electoral system will be incom-
plete which does not rest on universal adult suf-
frage; and that the malignant hatred of free speech
and right of meeting by the people evinced by the
House of Commons in passing the Parks Bill, and
also the treacherous manner in which the Govern-
ment seeks to administer the Act ( onfirms, more
than ever, the correctness of this opinion.
Mr. Cooper seconded, and Mr. Mooney sup-
ported, the resolution, which was carried un
mously.

The proceedings terminated at a quarter past
1, with a cordial vote of thanks to the Chairman.

articles.title: FRENCH TREATY AND THE "FREE BREAKFAST TABLE."
articles.text:
THE FRENCH TREATY AND THE
"FREE BREAKFAST TABLE."

The following is a copy of a letter and tele-
gram sent to Lord G-ranvillo on the 9th inst.
by Mr. T. Briggs :
"The Right Hon. Lord Granville, Minister for
Foreign Affairs.
_

"Mr LORD,—In these days of peace it is a
hard thing to see our rulers sowing the Beeis
of future wars with their eyes open to the in-
evitable consequences, so I deemed it my duty
to send you a telegram to the following effect,
viz., I have read the articles of the New
French Treaty of Commerce, and beg to be
allowed to enter my protest as being more in-
jurious to Great Britain and France than
could be inflicted in the event of -a' hostile
army, half a. million strong, landing at each
place, viz., Dover and Paris, hoping that by
so doing I might be the humble instrument in
the hands of God for preventing such a dis-
aster from being completed and ratified.
" Lbyalty to the Crown, the institutions,
and the people prompts me to this action, and
though I can scarcely expect any notice being .
taken of it by your lordship, I nevertheless
have the reflection that I have done my duty
to my neighbour as far as lay in my power.
'He that is in honour, and understandeth
not, is like the beasts that perish.'
"Will your lordship allow me to draw your
attention to the following manifest ham-
sistenoy, if not absolute absurdity, in the
preamble, viz., Her Majesty the Queen of
Great Britain, and his Excellency the Presi-
dent of the French Republic, being equally
animated with the desire to draw closer the
ties of friendship which unite their two Coun-
tries, and being desirous of placing on a per-
manent and satisfactory footing the commer-
cial relations between the two States, have
determined to conclude a treaty of commerce
and navigation, &c.'
"In the above there is a contradiction in
terms. How can 'the commercial relations
of the two countries be placed on a permanent
and satisfactory footing' under any commercial
treaty which interferes with the freedom of
exchange between the two countries or
peoples? M. Thiers has entered on a financial
policy or system by which he seems deter-
mined to complete the ruin of France; and I
would advise your lordship to withdraw from
such a position as will render your lordship
an accessory before or after the fact. .
"Commercial treaties are incompatible with
a free trade policy, and, as free trade is the first
condition to the bond of international peace,
let your lordship set about the work of clean."'
ing the hands of Great Britain, so that she
shall "touch not, taste not, handle not, the
unclean thing," and all other countries will,
in self-defence, and in the nature of things,
follow the example in God's good time."
