THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Tom Smith, aliag Kelly, a tramp, was
charged before the magistrate at Valley,
Bangor, on Monday with a murderous assault
at Presaddred on Friday. Prisoner presented
himself at the door of Captain King and begged
assistance. Being refused by the servant, he
struck her on the head with a hammer, nearly
killing her, and then, rushing into the house,
felled Captain King, who is 81 years of age, in
the same manner. A cry of murder from the
other female servants alarmed the assassin,
who decamped, and was not secured till
Saturday night. Prisoner, who has been pre-
viously convicted, was remanded.

In the Chamber of Commerce at Bradford
on Monday, Mr. Behrens complained that the
new French Treaty, so far as he could make
it out, many important passages being am-
biguously worded, would be very injurious to
the trade of Bradford. England, instead of
being the most favoured nation, would be the
least favoured up to 1876. Before coming to
any resolution, the Chamber decided to ask the
Foreign Office for explanations on some of
the doubtful clauses.

The snow-drift at Balmoral on Monday and
the greater part of Sunday was all but blind-
ing, and the snow now lies at considerable
depth. It is said that the Queen has ordered
her sledge to be put in readiness.

Iter Majesty the Queen of Holland left
Frampton Court, Dorchester, for London on
Monday morning.

It was resolved at the Glasgow Chamber of
Commerce on Monday to forward a memorial
to-her Majesty's Ministers praying for free
tra/le in banking as in other branches of trade,
and declaring that the monopoly of banking in
Scotland, created by the act of 1845, is
injurious alike to traders, manufacturers, and
depositors.

Eighteen charges arising out of the Licensing
Act disturbances came before the stipendiary
magistrates at Hull on Monday, and were
dealt with by sentences of imprisonment
ranging from tbirty days to six months. In
four oases there were options of fines varying
from 40s. to X 5.

At Manchester, a verdict of "Wilful murder
and suicide while in an unsound state of
mind" was returned on Monday, by the
coroner's jury against Annie Gurlin, 29, a
widow who poisoned herself and her little girl,
,-"Ada Millicent Gurlin, under three years of age,
by prussic acid on Saturday. The deceased
woman, who was greatly depressed in mind
after the loss of her husband recently, obtained
the poison a fortnight ago by falsely represent-
ing that she was the wife of a photographer,
and in this deception she was assisted by a
woman named Walker. The jury coupled with
their verdict a recommendation that Walker
should be prosecuted.

Colonel Holden, a supporter of Conservatism
and for many years in command of the South
Notts Yeomanry, died at Nottingham, on
Monday.

It transpired on Monday that the beautiful
lecternused in Sandringham Church on Sunday
was a thanksgiving memorial for the recovery
of the Prime of Wales, presented by the Princess
on his Royal Highness's birthday. The lectern
is in the form of a brass eagle with outstretched
wins, bearing on the breast a red cross, and
having beneath the inscription "To the glory
of God. A thank-offering, 14th December,
1871. Alexandra. When I was in trouble I
Called upon the Lord, and He heard me.'—
Psalm exx., verse 1."

Seven seamen, sent home under arrest by
the British consul at Bahia, were on Monday
charged at Southampton with attempting to
scuttle the ship John Prill, of Whitehaven, on
the high seas in August last. Seven attempts
*ere made during the voyage from Cardiff to
Bahia to sink the ship by boring holes in her,
and at last the captain, to intimidate the crew,
destroyed the only boat he had. Prisoners
were remanded, awaiting instructions from the
Board of Trade, who have the consul's depobi-

Prince Christian of Holstein arrived at
Dresden on Sunday with an autograph letter
from Queen Victoria congratulating the King
and Queen of Saxony upon the fiftieth anni-
versary of their wedding. The Emperor and
Empress of Germany left Dresden on Monday
evening.

The French Assembly met on Monday at
Versailles, and there was a good attendance of
*embers i , ncluding M. Thiers, M. Gambetta,
M. Rouher, the Due d'Aumale, and the Prinoe
de Joinvill:e. M. Grevy announced that he bad
received a letter from Prince Napoleon pro-
testing against his expulsion from France.
The letter was referred to the Petitions Com-
mittee, after some remarks from the member
for Corsica.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE.

The opening meeting of the Royal Geo-
graphical. Society's Session was held on Mon-
day evening at the London University. The
chair was occupied by Sir Henry Rawlinson,
the president, who, in his address, spoke of
Mr. Stanley's journey to Lake Tanganyika as
the most important geographical achievement
of the year, and one fully deserving the
Society's medal.

At Bow-streebioolice-court, on Monday (the
first day of hearing after Lord Mayor's Show
day), there were 52 charges of drunkenness;
at Clerkenwdl there were 46; and at Maryle-
bone 53.

Lord F. Cavendish presided at Leeds on
Monday at a meeting of the committee ap-
pointed to consider the proposed plans for esta-
blishing a College of Science at Leeds'.
Letters approving of the scheme were read
from. Colonel Akroyd, M.P., Sir T. Salt, Mr.
S. Beaumont, M.P., Mr. Morrison, M.P., and
others. The cost originally estimated was
£61,000; but the funds are not forthcoming,
and a committee was appointed to reconsider
the subject.

The Liverpool School Board on Monday
resolved to issue a precept on. the Town Council
for £1.7,702, to meet the balance of £3,702 due
to the treasurer on the last year's account, and
£14,000 for current year's expenses, compared
with £9,000 last year. A discussion arose as
to the character of the books used in the de-
nominational schools contributed to by the
Board, and as to whether images, symbols, or
emblems were used in teaching in those
schools. The subject was postponed for
further inquiry.

The Northumberland Coal Owners' Assooia-
tion on Monday advanced the price of small
coal from 258. to 30s. per chaldron. Very
recently the price of unsoreened coal was
reduced.

The apprehensions with regard to the health
of the Premier, which have been recently ex-
pressed, are, we are happy to state, without
foundation,

From Copenhagen we learn that Mr. Edward
Whymper' well-known for his feats of Alpine
climbing, has returned from a second jour-
.ney of exploration in North Greenland,
bringing with him a rich collection of curiosi-
ties, including some remarkable specimens of
fossilised wood.

Thomas Challoner, a oollier, was found dead.
on Monday on a cinder heap at Earl Gran-
villa's deep pit, Hanley. It is supposed that
he had laid down for the sake of warmth and
was suffocated by the fumes.

A. man named Michael Collis, who was dis-
charged from a lunatic asylum on Sunday
night, shortly afterwards set fire to a quantity
of furze in the neighbourhood of Limerick,
and placing himself in the midst, was roastqd
to death.

Professor Tyndall closed his lectures at
Boston with a speech from which we copy these
words:—" During my stay here I have heard
the old country mentioned amain and again.
You cannot abolish your antecedents. Out of
England's loins you have come. Your
ancestry is stamped upon your faces, your
laws, your politics, and your characters. De
Tocqueville, sympathising with Democratic
institutions, says, regarding England and
America—' I refuse to regard these people as
two. One is the outgrowth of the other.'
Atrocious ignorance of each other is at the
bottom of all our differences. I trust that
hereafter each nation will respect the indi-
viduality of the other, while thoroughly main-
taining his own."

The Sheffield Telegraph if: informed on the
best possible authority that the allegation made
that the "horse epidemic" had broken out at
Dronfield is unfounded. The horses alleged
to have been attacked by the epidemic are
.simply suffering from "catarrh fever."

Sir Watkin Wynn, Bart., M.P., is amongst
the Welsh members who have generously
subscribed to the Choir Fund.

At a numerously attended meeting of the
Cambridge University Boat Club, held on
Monday
.night, the President reported that he
had received a challenge from Oxford to row
the usual eight-oar race at the end of next
Lent term. It was resolved by acclamation
to accept the challenge; and the President and
Secretary are busily engaged in selecting
crews for the trial eights.

Mr. Fitzjames Stephen, Q.C., read before
the Social, Science Association, at its first meet-
ing for the season, a pa.per on the subject of
codification of the law. in India and in Eng-
land; tracing the history of cousolidatioa of
existing statutes in our great Eastern depen-
dency, and urging that all Indian experience,
while it taught valuable lessons as to the mode
of codification, pointed to the advantage of
such a proceas.

Letters of administration of the effects of
Maria Mangin. Brown, late of No. 28, Hert-
ford-street, Mayfair, who died on Dec. 21,
1871, a widow, without child or parent, brother
or sister, uncle or aunt, nephew or niece,
cousin-german, or any known relative, and in-
testate, has just been granted to John Grey,
Esq., the solicitor for the affairs of her Ma-
jesty's Treasury, for the use of her Majesty,
the personal property beinc, sworn miler
£250,000. By the death of this lady, without
leaving a will and without relations, this large
property—nearly a quarter of a million—falls
to the Crown.

The authorities of the Great Northern
Railway have now extended to their second
and third-class traffic comforts and advantages,
heretofore almost exclusively confined to first-
class passengers. The rolling stock has also
received the addition of a large number of new
third-class carriages, which are supplied with
foot warmers ,during the cold season, and
other appliances rendering them almost equal
to second-class Riches.

'T On Mondarn deputation had an interview
with the Lord Mayor, at the Mansion House,
their object being to request him to preside at
R public meeting of the citizens, on an early
day, for the purpose of protesting against the
further continuance of the income tax in its
present shape, or of-procuring its modification,
so that the taxtitien should be on realized
property, but not on property in course of
realization. The Lord Mayor intimated to
the deputation that he was willing to preside
at a public meeting on the subject, but be
wished it to be distinctly understood that he
would go there without at present giving any
opinion as to the objects of the deputation.
The deputation expressed themselves satisfied
with that intimation, which they thought
reasonable.

On Monday the Bavarian troops left the
camp at Chalons and occupied the barracks
which had been prepared for them at Vouziers,
Clermont, Verdun, and other places in the
Departments of the Ardennes and of the Meuse;
while the Prussian troops that occupied Rheims
have retired into the Meurthe, towards Nancy
and Pont- a-Mousson.

An application was made to the Court of
Queen's Bench, on Monday, to admit to bail
Mr. William Anderson, the head of a firm at
Liverpool, with branches at London, Glasgow,
Cork, and Waterford, whose business was of
great magnitude; he is in custody on a charge
of forging acceptances to a large amount, on
which advances had been made by the Com-
mercial Bank of Scotland. The court thought
there were no grounds for the application, and
accordingly refused to comply with it.

The importance of our torpedo defences has
been recognised by the appointment of a
second company of Royal Engineers specially
to be devoted to this branch of warfare, viz.,
the 33rd Company. of Royal Engineers, under
the command of Captain A. Parnell. This
company is shortly to be strengthened by
transfers from other companies at head-
quarters. Experiments will shortly be made
in the Medway.

On Tuesday. morning, at five o'clock, the
express train going north from Newcastle ran
into an engine and van at Heaton Junction, as
they were taking the points. The van was
carried some distance in front of the express
engine, until the latter got off the line com-
pletely disabled. The carriages, in passing
the other engine, had their handles and foot-
boards torn off. None of the passengers were
injured. The train was detained one hour.

One of the official organs of the Prussian
Government contradicts the statements pub-
lished as to the bill legalising civil marriage,
which was said to be not only prepared but to
have received Imperial sanction. This news
is altogether without foundation. "It is self-
evident," we are told, "that the present
Parliamentary crisis and the arrangement of
the Counties Bill must exclusively occupy the
attention of the Ministry of the State. Only
this pressing and mighty question has
been fully resolved will consultations take
place on the further legislative measures to be
laid before Parliament."

The foreign Governments to whom England
has addressed herself relative to the expedition
to Zanzibar have expressed their good wishes
for and sympathy with the undertaking, but
have not promised any active support.

On Menday night three of the crew of the
brig Sovereign of Whitby, Captain I.l‘Cartv,
arrived at the Sailors' Home, North Shields,
and reported that their vessel, while on the
homeward voyage from the Baltic to Wis-
beach, had sprung a leak during the gale on
Saturday, and one seaman was washed over-
board and drowned. The crew worked at the
pumps, but were obliged to abandon the
vessel waterlogged, and were picked up and
landed at Frederiekshaven, and subsequently
sent to Tyne.

Nov. 16, 1872.

An application was made at Rolls Chambers
on Monday to the Chief Clerk, on behalf of
the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone and Lord de
Tabby, as trustees under the will of the late
Duke of Newcastle, that a sum of £45,000,
the proceeds of the sale by private contract ofi
the mansion in Carlton House-terrace, should
be ordered to be invested in consols and allowed
to accumulate. The Chief Clerk made the
order asked for, hut remarked that he wished
now he had ordered the property to be sold by
public auction instead of by private contract.

A correspondent in New York says that
great inconvenience continues to be felt in that
city, owing to the epidemic among the horses.
More than half the street-cars and omnibuses
have been withdrawn, and the foreign steamers
leave with short cargoes because it is impos-
sible to convey goods from the warehouses to
the river. Oxen are being used in the city to
draw heavy drays, and the sight by its
novelty attracts crowds of idlers. Fortunately,
there has been little mortality among the
horses, and if .allowed a few days' rest they
generally recover from the disease—a kind of
severe influenza—from which they are suffer-
ing.

Two cases of violent assault upon the police,
were heard on Wednesday by the Hammer-
smith magistrate. In one of these the prisoner
was committed for trial without bail; in the
other, two men were fined 20s. and 40s. res-
pectively.

On Monday in the Court of Queen's Bench,
an application was made on behalf of the
Metropolitan Railway Company for a now trial
in the action lately brought against them by
Mrs. Swanborough, or to reduce the amount
of compensation awarded by the jury—Xl,6oo.
On August 2nd, 1871, the plaintiff, a well-
known aotresg, was seriously injured in a col-
lision at the South Kensington Station, a
severe cut upon the forehead being a material
ground on which she claimed damages. It
was contended for the company that the sum
given by the jury was excessive, but the
judges unanimously held that to an actress
the injuries received by Mrs. Swanborough
might tend to retard her professional pros-
pects, and tlierefore the rule for a new trial
was refused.

Sir Sydney Waterlow, the new Lord Mayor,
took his seat in the justice-room of the Man-
sion-honse on Monday, for the first time in
that capacity.

Mr. Bright, in declining an invitation to
attend a civic banquet at Birmingham, on
Saturday, wroth as follows:—" I am still
obliged to shun public dinners and meetings,
and speeches, and must therefore ask your
committee to excuse my absence, ram not
the less indebted to them for their kind re-
membrance of me."

The Court of Exchequer was on Tuesday
crowded by persons to witness the quaint
ceremony of nomination of sheriffs, which,
according to precedent, took -place on the
"morrow of St. Martin's Day." The nomi-
nation was for the counties of England and
Wales, except the royal duchies of Lancaster
and Cornwall: One gentleman begged to be
excused from serving on the shrievalty of
Cheshire on the ground of insufficient income
to meet the expenses of the office; and a
variety of reasons were urged by other gentle-
men to the Lords of the Council to be excused
from discharging the &Laos of sheriff for their
respective counties.

The Dublin Mail insists that the National
Board of Commissioners, in confirming the
sentence upon Father O'Keeffe, have esta-
blished a penal code against the liberties of
the priesthood as heinous as any penal law
ever levelled against that order; it assumes
that Parliament will never sanction such an
order.

In the matter of the Galway election
petition, voluminous informations have been
filed at Dublin against the defendants, lay and
clerical, who were recommended for prosecu-
tion by Judge Keogh. It is expected that the
venue will be changed from Galway to
Dublin. it is said that the several parties are
placed in the same position as if bills had been
found against them by a grand jury, and they
will be required to appear and plead with in a
certain number of days.

A. memorandum on the conduct of attack
by a division in the new drill formation has
been issued at Aldershot. The document goes
into minute particulars as to the employment
of the half-battalion in front and in flank
attacks' recommends a combination of both
methods of onset, and strongly impresses, on
the majors in command, the importance of
readily adapting their movements to the
exigencies of the moment, and acting on their
own independent judgment.

A telegram has been received in Jersey an-
nouncing the loss of the English- vessel John
Henry and, all bands.

Nov. 16, 1872

The Order in Counoil obtained by Mr.
Goschen, and which came into force at the
beginning of last month, has raised a storm
of dissatisfaction amongst the captains and
commanders of the royal navy. Mr. Goschen
has met their cry for increase of half-pay by
giving the captains an additional 2s. per day,
but at the same time he has struck off thirteen
out of the twenty-five good service pensions.
The number of the latter had been increased
from twenty by Mr. Childers during his tenure
of office.

In answer to an address from the Chamber
of Commerce, the Viceroy of India is stated
to have said that he objected to the transit
duty now levied on cotton at Kurrachee. The
export duty on grain and seed was less objec-
tionable. Its continuance would depend on
the general financial policy which would be
adopted next year, when he hoped there would
be a remission of taxation. He did not con-
sider it desirable that Soinde should be placed
under the Government of the Punjab.

In the Divorce Court on Tuesday afternoon,
before Registrars Owen and Middleton, in.
Chambers, an application was made by the re-
spondent for further time to file proofs in the
ease of Firebrace v. Firebraco. The solicitor
who appeared for the respondent said that the
matter had been delayed in the hope that an
amicable settlement would be come to; but as
there was no chance of any such result, he made
the application, in which the other side con-
curred, as they required a similar extension.
The time was granted as prayed for—viz., a
fortnight. Mrs. Firebrace now asks for a re-
stitution of conjugal rights.

A corredpondent in Rome says that the
sufferers by the late inundations in Italy need
help to an extent that neither the Government
nor private generosity will be able to provide;
it has accordingly been suggested that a sum
of about twenty millions of francs, collected
some years ago for the purpose of paying off
the National Debt by public subscription,
should be given to the devastated districts.
The proposal has been approved by the news-
papers of all shades of political opinion, and the
oa=etta d'ltalia has followed it up by recom-
mending that the amount assigned to the Pope,
which is lying idle because he has hitherto
refused to accept it, should be devoted to the
shine purpose.

Cardinal Cullen has addressed a letter to all
the Roman Catholic clergy of Ireland, desiring
them not to sign the new form of agreement
between managers and teachers of national
schools, issued by the Commissioners of Educa-
tion, and without which no school will be
entitled to share in the benefits of payment by
results, The Cardinal says, "Were we to
sign agreements which we do not perfectly
understand, we might perhaps sanction princi-
ples hostile to our interests, or calculated to
throw too much authority in educational
matters into the hands of men in power, some
of whom may be anxious to banish the influence
of religion from the school, and to rear up
youth in ignorance of, or indifference to, the
true faith."

Mr. Justice Denman will, at his own request,
be transferred from the Common Pleas to the
veteancy in the Queen's Bench arising from Mr.
Justice Rannen's appointment to the judgeship
of the Divorce Court.

During the week ending Saturday last, 5,585
births and 3,070 deaths were registered in
London and twenty other large cities and
towns of the United Kingdom. 'The mortality
from all causes in these towns was at the rate
of 22 deaths annually to every 1,000 persons
estimated to be living. In the metropolis
2,462 births and 1,118 deaths were registered,
the former having been 121 above, and the
latter 369 below the average. Fifteen persons
died from small-pox, 11 from measles, 14 from
scarlet fever, 3 from diphtheria, 25 from
whooping-cough, 28 from different forms of
fever, and 19 from diarrhcea.

From April Ist to the 9th instant the
Treasury receipts amounted to £41,287,396,
as compared with £36,691,918, in the corre-
sponding period of last year. The expenditure
has been £44,051,777. On Saturday last the
balance in the Bank of England exceeded
three millions and a half sterling.

On Tuesday about 400 labourers, including
their families, embarked at the London Doaka
for New Zealand, and another lot proceeded
to Liverpool, en route for Brazil. This week
there is increased activity in the Midlands
among emigration agents. Numerous meetings
are being held to enrol emigrants, and the rival
colonies are bidding high tor the exodus.

On Tuesday .evening Canon Gregory de-
livered the third and last of his second series
of lectures to young men in St. Paul's
Cathedral. There was a very numerous at-
tendance.

In consequence of the funeral of Genera'
Meade on Monday business was suspended at
Philadelphia.

At a meeting which has just been held. of
the Frenoh Conservatives, or party of the
Right, it was resolved to support Prince
Napoleon when his case comes before the
House, not from any personal sympathy with
the Prince, hut for political reasons.

M. Grevy was almost unanimously re-elected
President of the French Assembly and the
former Vice-Presidents were also re-elected,
the Left withdrawing the candidates it had
brought forward. General Changarnier's
question respecting M. Gambetta is to be
brought forward for discussion on Monday.

The Prussian Parliament was opened by the
Minister of War, on Tuesday, who read the
Speech from the Throne. The Speech, in re-
ferring to the Counties Reform Bill, recently
rejected by the Upper House, announced that
the measure had been somewhat modified, but
that its essential provisions were the same, and
that the Government was firmly resolved to
carry it by all the constitutional means at its
disposal. In the Upper House Count Stolberg,
a supporter of the Government, was elected
President by 79 votes out of 86.

An extraordinary application awaits the
judgment of Vice-Chancellor Malins. The
plaintiff, a lady named Ilaker,qmme into pos-
session of property worth £150,000, the whole
of which, except an annuity of £lOO, she was
induced by some means to entrust to a publican
named Loader, since deceased, to invest on her
account. The plaintiff knows nothing as to
what has become of her money, and the bill
is filed to obtain from the solicitor, or others
who acted for Loader, or were concerned with
him, a discovery of so much of it as still
remains.

A special meeting of the Leeds Liberal
Association has been called, to consider a
resolution to the following effect: "That all
Liberals should unite in demanding perfect
religious equality, household suffrage in the
counties, and economy in the naval expendi-
ture."

Lord John Manners, in presiding on Tues-
day evening at the dinner of the Licensed
Victuallers' Association at Leicester, said the
Act of last session appeared to treat mem-
bers of the trade as a common enemy, and to
place them on a footing somewhat lower than
that occupied by the slave-owners iu the West
Indian colonies, inasmuch as the former were
refused compensation for the sacrifice of their
property. He complained that the bill was
hurriedly push6d through Parliament, and in
the next session some remedial or explanatory
Act must be proposed, which might again
open the door to those honest fanatics and
dreaming visionaries.

A farmer named Connolly, residing at Mar-
shallstown, on the borders of Tipperary, has
been brutally murdered. On his way home
from Kilfinane, where he had been drinking,
he was met by a number of men, who set upon
him with sticks and knives, stabbing him in
several places. He died soon after being found.
A. man named Rourke is in custody on
suspicion.

A largely attended public meeting was held
in the Town Hall at Manchester, on Tuesday
night, in reference to the East African slave
trade. Mr. Birley, M.P., presided, and urged
the duty of Manchester to support the Govern-
ment in its measures to suppress the traffic.
The Rev. Horace Waller said the slave trade
at the present time was killing more people
than at any previous period in human history.
The traffic was increasing, and never was so
prosperous as now. Both he and the Rev.
Charles New gave thrilling accounts of the
horrors of the trade which had fallen under
their own observation.

A case arising out of the election at Oxford,
on Monday—a contest which continues to
cause a good deal of excitement—was brought
before the city magistrates on Tuesday. A.
lady was accused qf having shown her ballot-
forni to an alderman after having signed it.
Mr. Bendall, who made a statement to this
effeet, was asked to put it in writing for
further consideration.

Last week the total number of paupers in
the metropolis was 105,219, of whom 34,322
were in workhouses and 70,987 received out-
door relief. Compared with the years 1871,
1870, and 1869, these figures show a decrease
of 11,287, 28,532, and 33,017 respectively.
The number of vagrants relieved on the last
day of the week was 792.

A. boiler belonging to some saw mills in
Swan-street, Old. Kent-road, on Wednesday
exploded with great violence. Two persons
employed upon the premises were killed, many
others were injured, and much material
damage was done.

The liquidation arrangement in the case of
Mr. F. Strange having fallen through, pro.
ceedings in bankruptcy have been commenced,
and Mr. Sidney Smith, accountant, has been
appointed receiver to the estate.

A memorial to the Queen in Council for the
incorporation of Peterborough has been started,
and is being very numerously subscribed.

An inquiry was held on Wednesday by the
Inspector of the Local Government Board at
Rams..ate respecting some new powers sought
by the local board under the Ramsgate Im-
provement Act. The boatd sought especially
extra facilities for the collection of the coal
duty of 28. per ton by the erection of a weigh-
bridge—a form of taxation which the inspector
denounced as most cumbrous and inexpedient,
sufficient, if imposed for the first time, to
cause a revolt. The other alterations desired
were chiefly intended to simplify the mode of
procedure under the Public Health Act, and
some of them were opposed by the Ratepayers'
Protection Society.

Two eases under Extradition Treaties
one from Germany and the other from Belgium
—were heard at Bow-street on Wednesday.
In each of these a remand was granted.

In a letter to the Mayor of Newcastle, con-
veying the thanks of the Prince of Wales to
the people of that town for the address pre-
sented to him on the occasion of his recent
visit, Sir William Knollys says :—" It is
always a pleasure, his Royal Highness desires
to assure them, for him to visit the great
towns of England, and to have an opportunity'
of coming amongst the classes which so essen-
tially contribute to their prosperity. It is
orally a source of pleasure to him to identify
himself with the institutions of Englishmen,
and to labour, in common with his fellow-
countrymen, to hand them down unimpaired
to posterity.

M. de Soloyns, it is officially announced,
succeeds the late Baron Van der Weyer as
representative of the Belgian Kingdom at the
Court of St. James's.

At Lisbon, on Tuesday, authority was given
to add another important link to the ehaiu of
sub-oceanio telegraph communication—the
Portugese Minister of Public Works having
sanctioned the laying of a cable from Lisbon
to the Brazils, and of a duplicate cable from
Lisbon to England. The concessionaries are
the Falmouth, Gibraltar, and Malta Telegraph
Company, and the Telegraph Construction and
Maintenance Company.

Mr. Glyn met his constituents on Wednes-

A distressing maritime disaster is reported.
Early on Wednesday morning the Hiawatha,
bound from Bremerhaven to Falmouth, struck
on the Goodwin Sands, and was totally lost.
One of the crew was picked up, floating on
the cook-house of the wrecked vessel, off the
South Sand Head. The remainder of the

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 16, 1872.

THE RIGHT OF PUBLIC MEETING.

IN the course of a few days We shall have
long accounts of the proceedings taken against
Mr. ODGER and others, who, in defiance of Mr.
AYRTON'S prohibitions, dared to meet in Hyde
Park for the purpose of urging on the Govern-
ment the propriety of amnestying the Fenian
prisoners.

The right of public meeting and free speech
need not be regarded as requiring discussion
in the year of grace, 1872. The people of
England have stood up for this right and
always asserted it with a vehemence and de-
termination which prove the importance they

Nov. 16, 1872.

attach to it. It is exercised by every class of
the community, and it is brought to the aid of
every conceivable description of enterprise.
The hardiest stickler for an authority in
Government or the most ignorant operative
Conservative could. scarcely be brought to
deny the people's right in this matter ; and
it is, therefore, our duty to consider what such
a concession to right can be worth if Mr.
AYRTON or any other official be allowed to
practically override it, by the provisions of an
Act of Parliament, hurriedly pushed through
its various stages, for no purpose on earth but
to put down large gatherings of the people,
always detestable to men in office who are
anxious to escape criticism.

The "particular question of a Fenian
amnesty has nothing to do with the matter
in dispute. It is the old question as to the
right to meet in the parks in another form.
It is not a naked attempt to override this
right ; it is what is far more offensive—a
cunning device to so far control it as to take
away its value. The necessity for preventing
this by every possible means is obvious, as if,
in this matter, Mr. AYRTON gets his way the
right of working men to meet in London in
such numbers as to show their earnestness and
unity of decision will be practically de-
stroyed.

How is it to bo exercised if any Jack-in-
Office can hold up his finger, and order the
working people otf such open spaces as they
may think proper to assemble in? The Hole-
in-the-Wall was shut against meetings by the
dicta of the licensing magistrates, and it was
only when the landlady took a loyal title for
her hostelry, and promised future amendment,
that she was allowed to carry on her business.
The publicans, always, more or less, under the
ban of the virtuous portion of the community,
know that they are very much at the mercy of
the police and the magistrates, and will not,
therefore, encourage gatherings by which they
are brought under suspicion, and through
which they may be ruined. Small local rooms
are out of the question, not only because of
their expense, but because meetings held in
such places are seldom, if ever, noticed in the
newspaper press, and, therefore, have little or
no influence on public opinion. In fact,
except for purposes of organization, swill
local meetings are of little use. The
halls which may be had for the hiring
are now frequently closed against meet-
ings where unfashionable opinions are
uttered, as the shutting up of St. George's
Hall, last Sunday night, will serve to show.
The proprietors of such places know that if
they open their doors to those who oppose a
strong middle or upper class prejudice, they
have to pay a penalty in pecuniary loss which
few can afford to incur. It is true that
Exeter Hall and St. James's Hall can be had
when not otherwise engaged, but at a price
absolutely ruinous to working men, some-
where about £6O being the cost of a public
meeting in these places.

What is there, we ask, left for the accommoda-
tion of large gatherings of working men if the
parks are closed? It is true they can meet in
Hyde Park, leave being asked and obtained,
and a number of uncalled-for and troublesome
conditions submitted to. The handing in of
speakers' names, and the illegality of any man
opening his mouth, if this has not been done,
is a decree which could only have originated
in the most arrogant official wantonness. Such
a provision will, we are sure, never be sub-
mitted to, and for the working men of London
to attempt to act in conformity with it would
be equivalent to an abdication of their rights
as free citizens. We know there are in Lon-
don, as elsewhere, intemperate men, but we
cannot submit to a general gagging and
snaffling because this is the case. It is a pity
that the nerves of fine people should be dis-
turbed by coarse language, but such a thing
furnishes no justification to Mr. AYRTON in
running an official bit into people's mouths
and fastening on a tight Government curb.

We have no hesitation in calling on the
public to resist the petty and vexatious ty-
ranny of such a law, and we hope that our
London working men will offer it every kind
of legitimate resistance, and in such a case
almost any form of resistance will be legiti-
mate. It i 3 a positive disgrace to the Govern,

Nov. -16, 1872.

ment, and to the House of Commons that such
a law was ever passed, and it will be a greater
disgrace still to the voters of the Tower Ham-
lets if they do not drive its author from
amongst them in ignominious defeat. Mr.
GLADSTONE is really risking his position by
permitting such conduct on the part of his
subordinates, and if at the next election his
party suffer defeat he may ascribe it rather to
his own want of courage and lack of sym-
pathy with the general public than to any
miserable going back of public thought in the
guise of a Conservative reaction.

articles.title: ELECTORAL REFORM.
articles.text:
ELECTORAL REFORM.

TIIE Conference held at St. James's Hall has
made a good beginning. It took a right tone,
and, as a first manifestation, gave fair promise
of combining the sorts and varieties of material
requisite for success. He must he a very
short-sighted statesman who imagined that the
new Reform Act, when followed by the Ballot,
would crown the edifice of representative
perfection. On the contrary, they could but
be stepping-stones towards that end, an end,
perchance, which cannot even now be reached
by one more stride, however bold and
vigorous. While a quasi-household suf-
frage and the secret vote arc most
certainly points ofjvantage which encourage
us to make another spring, their immediate
practical effect is to set in more glaring light'
the vast inequalities, the insufferable dispro-
portions that remain untouched; nay, that,
instead of being diminished in the least degree,
have been greatly aggravated by the increase
of the electoral body in populous boroughs,
without, on the one hand, any proportionate
increase in the number of representatives to be
returned from such boroughs, and without, on
the other, any sensible reduction in number
or in right of those politically contemptible
little places that are still suffered to send up
to Parliament as many members, borough for
borough, as boroughs bigger than a dozen of
them; and that, as a class of Parliamentary
boroughs by themselves, form a total the figure
of which is a standing insult to the population,
wealth, and intelligence of the rest of the
British community.
Mr. KNATCHIIIILL-11IIGESSEN, in "Mac-
millan's Magazine," clearly shows that in our
borough system we reverse the principle that
the intelligent must rule. Three millions and
a half of people in London have twenty-two re-
presentatives. In seventeen great towns,
3,270,000 have thirty-seven, in twenty-two
towns, with over 1;0,000 inhabitants each,
1,575,000 people have also thirty-seven. In
fifty-four towns, over 20,000, 1,850,000, have
eighty-one. In ninety-five other towns,
952,000 have a hundred and twenty votes.
The borough of Marylebono alone has 477,555
inhabitants; fifty-six small boroughs have
400,000; yet these little towns have fifty-six
votes, while the great London borough has
only two. In fact, the franchise is given to
the people with one hand, and taken away
from them by the other.
No doubt, this preposterously outrageous
state of things subsists for no other or better
reason than that no sufficient combined effort
has been made to sweep it away. Besides this,
however, it is to be remarked, that, in the
only real effort that was over made, there was
a want, not merely of broad combination, but
of practical sense. The idea of geometrically
equal electoral districts was chimerical, one of
the reasons, no doubt, that it commanded no
union of classes for its furtherance. No doubt,
for a just distribution of electoral power, the
principle of equality, or some practical appli-
cation of it, is required, and there is as little
question that it might be attained, with at
least a pretty close approximation to exactness
in all substantial and appropriate respects.
The more the subject is contemplated, the
wider it opens to the view. Not simply must
we go forward; we must likewise make good
the ground already gained. Household suf-
frage must be made what at present it too
much only pretends to be; and the lodger
franchise will be in danger of going out alto-
gether, so far as labour is concerned, unless it
be freed from all the uncertainties and teasing
difficulties with which it is at present ham-
pered. Of what use to give men votes, and not
to afford them due opportunity of recording

them: to tantalize one man, might conceivably
be a fair punishment for foul offence ; but to
tantalize the bulk of a great people, for no
fault at all, but under pretence of giving them
a boon, is pure mockery and by no means safe.
Moreover, in any conceivable shape, a redis-
tribution of seats might prove a complete ex-
clusion of working men from a seat in
Parliament, unless accompanied by every
facility which impartiality claims and inde-
pendence might accept.

articles.title: PRUSSIAN CRISIS.
articles.text:
THE PRUSSIAN CRISIS.

THE BISMARCRIAN energy has not been
exhausted and is not to be deterred. The
Berliners are on the tiptoe of expectation for
great, if not startling events; and the Liberals
are described as full of hope and wise in
union. On the one hand, the Tory party hint
at concession, and the House of Notables have
chosen for their President by a very large
majority Count STOLBERG, a Government
man; on the other, the Minister of COM-
MERCE, the only member of the Cabinet who
disliked the rejected Bill, is spoken of as
likely to retire from office. The speech from
the Throne, on the opening of the new
session, read, mark, by the °, MINISTER
for WAR, promises two measures as,
among others, mainly declaratory of the
Government policy. One is "on the relation
of the State to Religious Houses," which
touches on subjects respecting which the
Prussian Government seems not less decided
than the Grand Council of Geneva, and per-
Imps even more so than the Italian Ministry.
But yet more important, as to immediate
issues, at least, than this, will be the Bill to
be substituted for the recently rejected
measure. The Diet are firmly apprised that
the prinoipal task which they will be called
upon to undertake is, the re-construction of
the administration of the districts or counties.
This, it is intimated, will involve the solution
of other questions. Moreobseurely, but not less
ominously, it is declared, that, besides main-
taining the chief proposals of the former Bill,
certain alterations will be introduced, the ex-
pediency, nay, the necessity for which has
been shown by former debates. In a tone
which reminds us of our "Iron D TrKE's "
famous saying, that "there should be no
mistake," the Speech closes with the expressed
resolution of the Government to avail itself
of every constitutional means at its disposal.
Prince BISMARCIC may be a politician more
than he. is a patriot, and is certainly a man of
expedients rather than of principles; but we
shall be greatly mistaken if he do not prove
himself the lay LUTHER that we have
prophesied, and, treading down priests with a
decisive foot, build up Germany and hold her
out before Europe in harmony with the
national intelligence and the national will.

IRON MOULDERS' MONTHLY REPORT.
THE monthly reports published by 'certain
of our principal trades unions are really very
useful documents, and might, we think, be
rendered more useful still if some joint plan
could be agreed on in regard to the general
matter they contain. The engineers, the
carpenters, the iron founders, and other trades
publish these documents, and although they
are devoted to the concerns of the special
bodies by which they are published, there
can be no reason why, by common arrange-
ment, they might not contain the highest and
best teaching as regards the principles and
practices of trades unionism. In fact, lessons
on political economy written in view of the
rights and interests of working men. We
make these remarks because we have noticed
in the iron founders' circular of the present
month, a very useful and encouraging address
to the members of that,body, signed by Messrs.
MORTON, GUILE, and Woons. This document
not only contains a statement of account, but
it speculates on the causes by which the trade
is influenced, and states why it is slightly
slacker now than it has been for some time
past, and why in the course of a few months
activity may again be expected to return, and
in this way usefully prepares the minds of the
men for such changes as may be fairly looked
for. This is in itself an admirable feature,
but the address goes ,beyond this, and urges
the men to resist stoutly any attempt that

may be made to take back from them the
shortened day so recently obtained.
Such advice on the various points in which
the members ot tbe society are interested,
given at regular intervals would have a good
effect, and if given generally in some prepared
document which appeared in all the monthly
circulars, would put a unity of thought into
the whole of our trades movement which,
through the members of these unions, would
gradually find ,its way out amongst working
men generally, greatly to the advantage of the
labour cause.

For ourselves, we have no fear that the
shortened day will be taken back. Still it is
quite right that Mr. DANIEL GUILE and his
friends should counsel watchfulness in regard
to it, as everything gained by the movements
of men in union should be made secure by
adding conquest to conquest, and giving back
nothing, till the emancipation of labour had
been thoroughly accomplished. To outsiders
these little trades papers are of great value, as
we are instructed by the information they con-
tain, and encouraged by the intelligence and
sound business experience they give proof of
in the men who issue them.

articles.title: HOW TO RESIST THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER.
articles.text:
HOW TO RESIST THE AGRICULTURAL
LABOURER.

TILE Newmarket farmers have determined
to take the field against the exorbitant de-
mands of the agricultural labourers. More
than seventy gentlemen have already joined
their union, and if the oppressions complained
of by these gentlemen are felt as acutely by
others of their class, this association may soon
spread itself all over the country.
There are two points to which they mean
specially to direct their attention. One is to
convince the labourers that the statements of
the " agitator 2 ' are fallacies; and the next to
resist anything like " compulsion " in regard
to the amount of wages to be paid. They are
quite satisfied that the price of labour should
be of their fixing, and that any attempt on the
part of the man who has the labour to sell is
an offence which should be opposed and
punished. The present demand of the labourers
—stimulated by the "agitators "—is 14s. per
week, and time to be allowed for breakfast; a
claim which the Newmarket farmers seem bound
to oppose by a powerful organization supported
by a rate of 10. in the pound to meet the ex-
pense.

Of course, the farmers' friends of the old
typo will back up this league of British yeo-
men. We shall be having speeches at agricul-
tural dinners to prove the unreasonableness
and extravagance of this demand, which we
doubt not will find record in the good old
county journals. We shall also have clever
men of figures proving, by aid of the multipli-
cation table, bow such a concession, if forced
upon the farmers, must inevitably lead to their
ruin.

We must confess that one of the items in
the labourers' demand does look unreasonable.
We do not see why men whose only mission on
earth seems to be to work and starve, should
insist on having a breakfast time. The first
consideration with them should be how to get
the breakfast, but if they are satisfied that the
Hs. per week will give them a chance of
getting it they 'aught certainly have some
little time allowed in which to eat it.
However, if the statists do step forward in
aid of the farmers there are one or two BUM
which we should like them to work out; not
only because of the light they might throw on
the subject for the general public, but also be-
cause they might be of advantage to the
labourer in instructing him how to economize
his means. If with the assistance of the
"dietary tables" of the various workhouses
they would draw up a bill of fare, not for food
alone, but for clothes, house-rent, firing,
medicine, and all else wanted by, say, a
family of three—a man, his wife, and one
child—and show how these things may be
comfortably provided for 12s. per week, the
document would be outious as well as in-
structive. Of course, our statists should not
forget the perquisites "in kind" which the
labourer gets from his employer, nor should
they, on the other hand, overlook loss of
wages through sickness, bad weather, or any
other disabling casualty to which the labourer

is subject. We only want the best informa-
tion we can get, and from men of figures we
ought to look for this with much confidence.
It would not be necessary in drawing up this
table to make it quite as costly as a workhouse
diatery, inasmuch as the British labourer has
always lived worse than a British pauper,
and therefore minimized quantities will not be
felt by him as a hardship. As for the bills of
fare in our prisons these must be put entirely
aside as preposterously beyond the expectations
of honest labourers. Or perhaps a nice little
tract got up for extensive circulation amongst
the labouring poor in the agricultural dis-
tricts, entitled, "How to support a family on
12s. per week," would have a better effect.
We only throw out the hint, and leave the
Newmarket gentlemen to settle amongst them-
selves the best way of carrying it out. It is
quite clear that something ought to be done,
or the extravagant and ruinous sum of 14s.
may be insisted on and obtained.
The position of the country at the present
moment, owing to the "agitators" no doubt,
is very critical. Tha franchise for farm
labourers has already been asked for, and that
once obtained there will be nothing for the
landowners but to emigrate, to take their land
out of the country, and put it down where
they can make it more profitable than under
the appalling demands made it can be.
We have been told for a long time that manu-
facturers would take their capital out of tho
' country, and invest it where trades unions
could not interfere to prevent them from mak-
ing legitimate profits; and though they have
not carried out the dreadful threat, the land-
lords may, in a fit of righteous indignation,
run away with their broad-acres, and anchor
them in some far off sea where Coolie labour
may be easily procured. Should they not do
this, then the English labourer had better insist
that whilst he is called on to cultivate these
acres he must be properly paid for doing it,
even though those above him should have to
moult some of their fine feathers for the pur-
pose of increasing the supply of bread and
meat on his table.
We have no hesitation in telling the land-
lords and farmers that they have an ugly time
before them if they enter on a strong agitation
against their labourers. The people of Eng-
land—the working people—respect property
and its owners, but the labourers on the land
must not be driven to emigration as the only
escape from starvation. Whilst respecting pro-
perty we must not forget to protect life, and
to save our country, at the same time, from
depopulation. How to do this is a tough pro-
blem, but with the help of GOD and the
" agitator " it will be solved.

articles.title: BURNING OF BOSTON.
articles.text:
THE BURNING OF BOSTON.

Tuz youngest of the great American cities
was not long ago destroyed by fire. A like
fate has now befallen the oldest. (Some of the
lessons taught by the former calamity are re-
inculcated by the present. Materials too
hastily supposed to be proof against heat are
found to become powder under its influence.
Iron itself is subject to such conditions, from
heat and from cold, and from the alternations
of the two, as call in question its Claim to fire-
proofness, while, as is found in such examples
as our own Thames-street flour-mill, and the
Cramton iron bridge across the, deep South
Wales Valley, its dilation and contraction
under varieties of temperature oven beneath
the open sky, still more from actual fire fol-
lowed by water, incurs peculiar perils demand-
ing the utmost care during ordinary circum-
stances, much more in sudden emergencies.

It is a comfort that few deaths have occurred
at Boston, and not many families been made
houseless. The destruction of warehouses and
their contents has, however, been ruinously
great. As to loss of property in goods, the
time was unfortunate, stocks of all kinds being,
from circumstances, unusually large. The lire
offices of Boston are naturally the chief suf-
ferers; but the same effect will try the offices
of New York; and some half-dozen English
offices will be largely drawn upon; for, in
addition to the necessary tendency of American
firms to take out British policies, a number of
warehouses and their contents reduced to ashes
were the property of manufacturing firms in
this island. The Boston offices Aro /*pre"

10

seated. as unable to pay more than half the
amounts they had eagerly assured. But the
SECRETARY to the TREASURY has promised
such assistance as will prevent anything like
a suspension of payments or commercial panic.
The Government of Italy, we observe, mean
to apply to the relief of the sufferers from
floods the twenty millions of frates formerly
collected by public subscription for paying off
the National Debt. This is their answer to
the mocking taunt of the priests that the
calamity is an expression of the Divine anger
against the ICING and Parliament, which an-
swer will be made finely pointed should the
money assigned to the Pork:, but lying idle
because he sulkily refused to take it, be also
devoted to the same more useful purpose.
The merchants and the fire offices of Boston
will, no doubt, weather the storm of fire that
has overtaken them, at the same time learning
the lesson that it teaches. The firemen found
many of the warehouses so lofty that the
water barely reached the top, though it was
their wooden' roofs that mainly carried the
flames from street to street. Neither granite
nor marble can be relied upon for resistance
to heat; while the bulk of the materials of
the consumed blocks was stone and iron,
and even the unfinished new Post-office, com-
posed of granite and iron, without any wood
at all, though not positively burned, ha S suf-
fered so much injury from continguity to the
flames that a great part of the building will
have to be pulled down and renewed, the" old
South Church," at first reported as destroyed,
and described as "a venerable brick building,"
Was, it seems, left entirely uninjured. The
city contains many historical edifices, of which
this is one; and it is a solace to the citizens
who pride themselves on their direct descent
from the "Pilgrim Fathers," to be able to
announce that no structure of a monumental
character has been consumed.

It is a useful though a trite reflection on
such calamities, that in men of a money type
they give a spur to enterprise, while suggest-
ing unthought-of improvements, and. main-
taining the demand for labour, and every other
saleable commodity.

articles.title: OVERWORK ON RAILWAYS.
articles.text:
OVERWORK ON RAILWAYS.

The Bishup of Manchester was present at a
soiree of railway servants at Manchester, in connec-
tion with the City Mission, and in the course of
his address to the men made a remark upon their
hours of labour. —lie said he had asked Mr. Tootal,
one of the directors of the London, and North-Wes-
tern Railway, how long the company expected one
engine-driver to drive his eng:ne without rest;
and Mr. Tootal had answered that two hours was
the time. The Bishop thought, however, that
the safe.ty of a railway train depended upon
pointsmen even more than upon drivers; and if he
was perched up in a cabin with about 25 points in
front of him, he was afraid he would be very
much in the mune position as the pointsman of
Muddleby Junction, of whom a cartoon appeared
in Punch a short time ago. Seeing, therefore,
that the work of a pointsman was so difficult, he
considered that four hours was as long a time as a
pointstuan, while at work, could carry a clear
brain.

• Mr. James Bancroft, one of the directors of the
London and North-Western Railway, begged
leave to say that, if his lordship was put into a
signal-box to work the points, having the power
of abstraction that he had, he would kill half the
passengers in the country. Mr. Bancroft held
that no man capable of abstraction was fit for a
peintsman. Those particular railway officials
must have but one idea and one object. Tho com-
panies, therefore, seleoted, to work the points, a
particular class of men who were capable of pursu-
ing their work longer than any other men what-
ever would be. The London and North-Western
Company, he was proud to say, made it a point
that their servants should have an onortunity of
attending a place of worship at least once a Sab-
bath, and had passed a solemn resolution that the
railway should not be worked on Sabbaths•more
than was really demanded by the necessities of the
Public. The directors believed their arrangements
were as nearly perfect as they could be ; and
when accidents occurred they submitted to be
abused, saying they had done their best.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOUR QUES-
TION.

A meeting of farmers was held on Tuesday at
Newmarket, at which it was annotmeed that more
than 70 gentlemen, had, given in their names as

members of a proposed Agricultural Association to
resist strikes and the efforts of professional agita-
tors. The speakers disowned the slightest desire
to act in an oppressive way, and stated that their
wish was to convince the labourers-of the fallacies
of the statements of agitators, and while advanc-
ing wages as much as was justifiable, resist any
attempt at compulsion. The origin of the meeting
was a demand of the labourers for 14s. per week,
and time to be allowed for breakfast. Rules for
the government of the association were adopted,
and it was decided to levy a rate of lid. in the
pound to meet the expenses. A meeting of
labourers to form a Union for Cambridgeshire will
be held next week, and a similar meeting to
establish an Agricultural Labdurers' Union for
West Suffolk.

articles.title: FIRE AT BOSTON.
articles.text:
THE FIRE AT BOSTON.

According to the latest information received
here, the great fire at Boston has devastated about
eighty acres, covered with the best wholesale
housee in the city. From 700 to 800 buildings
have been destroyed, including all the principal
"dry goods" establishments, as well as the wool
and leather houses, filo or six savings banks, and
Trinity Church. It is believed that not more
than 200 persons have been rendered homeless, for
very few dwelling-houses were consumed. There
was an unusually large stock of dry goods on
hand, as the sales during the season just closing
had been light, and fresh stocks of linens, cottons,
and other fabrics for summer wear had recently
been taken in. The wool market also has been
dull, so that immense quantities of that staple had
accumulated, Boston baying had more than any
other American city. All this has been destroyed.
Pearl-street, which has been ,devastated by the
flames, was the chief market of the New England
shoe ancl leather trade.

,•A meeting of the Board of treclermiters has
been held, and it was estimated that the total loss
would be 250,000,000 dols., most of which falls
on Boston insurance companies. It is feared that

many of them will be unable to bear this heavy
strain on their resources. All were eager to take
risks on the class of property destroyed. The
burned buildings, almost without an exception,
were granite, iron, or freestone. Not one is left
standing Within the district over which the fire
extended. The granite especially crumbled to
pieces.

About 25 persons are supposed to be buried
under the ruins. The progress of the fire in
Water-street was stopped by the unfinished post-
office and the premises of the Post newspaper.
The former is granite and iron. No wood what-
ever was used; yet nearly half of that part of the
building which was next the fire will have to be
pulled down.
In Washington-street the flames were stopped
by the old South Church, a venerable brick build-
ing which, it seems, is uninjured. State-street,
with its principal banks, sustained no damage ;.but
the rear of the principal Post-office was burned.
The mails were removed in safety to Faneuil Hall.
None of the historical localities were reached by
the flames.

Much shipping was destroyed, but the vessels
were chiefly coasters.
When the firemen got to work, it was found
that many of the warehouses were so high that
the water barely reached the top ; and the Man-
sard roofs of wood, so common in Boston, carried
the fire with rapidity from street to street.
No disorders occurred, there being a large mili-
tary force on duty, with police from all the neigh-
bouring towns, and firemen from all parts of New
England.

THE CHURCH DEFENCE ASSOCIATION.

At a meeting held in the Town Hall, Birming-
ham, on Thursday evening last, by the Church
Defence Association, the Rev. J. 3. Manley, in the
course of his speech, made the following remarks:
—The Dissenting Press, both in London and the
provinces, had flooded the whole kingdom with
tracts and pamphlets, and printed things innumer-
able, which crawled upon the face of the country,
full of-41. Voice—" Lies ")—what they called
facts, regarding this question. A friend had
anticipated the very word he was afraid to use,
but he had hit the nail on the head. They were
lies—at least, the majority of them. (Hear,
hear). Let him give them one or two instances.
Mr. George Potter, a gentleman, who, he believed,
for filthy lucre's sake, as well as having a ready
mind, stumped the country on behalf of the Libe-
ration Society, last February, had said at Burton-
on-Trent in a lecture that the clergyman of St.
Bride's, Fleet-street, London, was in receipt of
£2,000 a year or £BO for each attendance. And
the people cried " Shame, shame." No wonder
it was a shame," said Mr. Potter, "for ten millions
of money to be subscribed to the Church of Eng-
land when only one-third of the people attended
her services. It was unfair for Parliament to vote
such a sum out of the revenue of the country,
besides giving to the bishops the privilege to sit
in the House of Lords."

To this attack of the rev. gentleman Mr. George
Potter replied by a letter which appeared in the
Birmingham Post on Monday last, of which the
following is the material portion
"To this untruthful and ungentlemanly attack
permit me to say :
" Firstly,—That I have never spoken at 'Bur-
ton-an-Trent ' on the question.
"Secondly,—That I have never in my life stated
that the vicar of St. Bride's was getting £2,000
a year.'
"Thirdly,—That I have never said 'that Par-
liament voted £10,000,000 a year to the Churela
out of the taxes.'

"Fourthly,—That I indignantly deny having
stumped the country for filthy lucre's sake.'
"Fifthly,—That these untruths which the Rev.
Y. S. Manley uttered on Thursday have appeared
before, and were broadly and directed contradicted
by me at the time. They were falsehoods then,
and still remain so.

•
"In conclusion, let me remark that if the other
statements made by this rev. and Christian minister
in his speech are as incorrect as the above, what
credit does he gain, or what does he confer on the
noble and sacred cause' which he defends r'

articles.title: ALEXANDRA. PARK.
articles.text:
ALEXANDRA. PARK.

Alderman Sir Sills John Gibbons asks us to
publish the following letters and resolution,
as explanatory of what has transpired between
Messrs. Markby and Tarry, Mr. Charles
Lucas, and himself :
" Mansion House, London, 8.C., Oct. 30.
" Sir,—l am requested by the Lord Mayor
to call your attention to the tone of the public
Press with reference to the Guarantee Fund
which his Lordship has instituted as a means
of complying with your stipulation of securing
to the proprietors of the Alexandra Park
property the sum* of £lOO,OOO in the event of
an agreement being entered into for the pur-
chase of this property.
"By this you will not fail to observe that
the whole of the editorial articles are in favour
of his Lordship's proposal, provided the terms
of purchase shall be agreed on before the meet-
ings of the 4th November next, but not other-
wise.
"It therefore occurs to the Lord Mayor that
you will be consulting the best interest of
yourself and the other owners of the property,
as well as materially lightening the labours of
his Lordship, if you will allow him to state
publicly on the 4th of November the terms on
which you will be willing to sell the property
to the public.
"I may state that the Lord Mayor has con-
vened two meetings, by publics advertisement,
for the 4th of November, at the Mansion
House—one at 4 o'clock in the afternoon,
when he has invited his brother citizens to aid.
the cause; and the other at 7 o'clock in the
evening, when the people are invited to ex-
press their opinion upon the subject, with the
sole view of raising the money necessary to
pay for the property at the earliest possible
date. His Lordship has also convened a
meeting for the 6th of November, at the
Mansion House, at which the co-operation of
the ladies is invited, having the same object
in view.
"If this proposal of his Lordship is agree-
able to you, he will be happy to receive you
here on Friday next at 11 o'clock, to discuss
the terms and conditions of sale and purchase.
"I have the honour to subscribe myself,
"Yours obediently,
" Joni% Gisus, Private Secretary.
"Mr. C. T. Lucas."

To this letter Sir Sills Gibbons received no
reply, but on the 4th of September a letter
was received at the Mansion House from
Messrs. Markby and Tarry, which, in conse-
quence of Sir Sills having to preside at three
public meetings on that day, was not opened
by him until the morning of the sth, on whit:di
day he wrote the following reply
ALRVANDRA. PARK.
Mansion House, London, B.C. Nov. 5.
" Gentlemen,—l am requested by the Lord
Mayor to reply to your letter of the 4th inst.
by stating that the letter you refer to as
having been sent by Messrs. Lucas and Borra-
dello on the 16th of October has not been re-
ceived by his Lordship. A copy of that letter,
however, was received by him on the evening
of the Slat.

" With reference to the proposed purchase
of the property, I am directed to enclose copy
'of a resolution which was passed yesterday at
the meetings at the Mansion House, by which
you will perceive that no further steps are to
be taken to complete the Guarantee Fund
until the terms of sale are communicated to the
Lord Mayor.
"His Lordship is of opinion that, if the
owners require only reasonable terms, a meet-
ing between the& and the Sub-Committee
would lead to an issue satisfactory to all
parties concerned, as the Committee are pre-
pared to enter into a contract of purchase which
will ensure payment for the property before
possession is given.
"Your clients should always bear in mind
that the Lord Mayor and Committee have no
personal interest whatever to serve beyond
acquiring the property for the people on fair
terms, and, at the same time, to meet your
clients' wishes of receiving the purchase-money
at the earliest possible date.
4,1 remain, Gentlemen, your
obedient servant,
" JOSEPS °lnns.
"Messrs. Markby and Tarry, 57, Coleman-
street."

" Copy of resolution passed at the Mansion
sion House meeting, November 4. Moved by
Mr. Henry Hoare, seconded by Mr. Frederick
Young
• "That further action in the matter of the
guarantee stand in abeyance until the owners
of the property have named a price to the
Lord Mayor, as many gentlemen have declined
to support the Guarantee Fund until this is

articles.title: Nov. 16, 1872
articles.text:
Nov. 16, 1872

HOUSE ACCOMMODATION FOR THE
LONDDN POOR.

A public meeting was held on Monday even-
ing at the Workmen's Club, Cow-cross, Smith-
field, to protest against the wholesale d.emoli-
tim of the homes of the poor, and to demand
the erection of more suitable house accommo-
dation.
Via. John Bennett was called to the chair, and
in opening the proceedings he said Parliament
had, year after year of late, passed Acts
authorising railway companies to brine. their
lines into the City. Clauses sere inserted in
most of all those Acts that the companies
should set apart land for the erection of other
houses in the place of those which were taken
down; but those clauses were permissive only,
and the result was that the railway companies
did not carry them out. Of late something
had been done to meet the great want
which existed of more house accommodation
for the poor. There was the Peabody Insti-
tution and the Society for the Erection of
Dwellings for the Poor, of which the present
Lord Mayor was the moving spirit. The Cor-
poration of the City of London had also ex-
pended £60,000 with the same objeot. When
the Metropolitan Improvement Bill was before
Parliament Sir Sydney Viraterlow induced the
Corporation to procure the insertion of a
clause not only that use might be made of the
vacant spaces, but which required that within
three years the Board of Works should secure
a site for the erection of dwelling-houses in
the place of those demolished. There was a
piece of land now vacant which extended from
Field-lane to Ely-place which was available
for the purpose, and the only question was
who were the parties to erect the buildings.
About £lO,OOO would be required to cover
this piece of ground with dwellings for the
working classes, and the Lord Mayor told him
that either his Company or the Improvement
Committee of the Corporation of the City of
London would be prepared to take the matter
in hand, and to do all that was required in the
best possible way, and he suggested that a
deputation should. be appointed by the meeting
to wait on the Lord Mayor.
Mr. Catlin moved the first resolution
That this meeting does solemnly protest against
the wholesale demolition of houses in the metro-
polis for the making of railways and metropolitan
improvements without making provision for the
thousands of persons who are driven from their
homes.
He said that as a City missionary he was well
acquainted with the homes of the poor of
London. The great want of the day was homes
for poor working people. The large palatial
buildings which had been erected with that
view were of no uso to the poor man, who out
of 15s. a week of weekly earnings could not
pay a rent of ss. 6d. a week. He suggested
that buildings should be erected with fiats
similar to those in Edinburgh.
Mr. George Brooke, a member of the
Clerkenwell Board of Guardians, seconded the,
motion. It was important, he remarked, that
artisans should live 'near their work. He
reminded the meeting that some years ago, by
the improvements in Paris, the artisans were
driven into the suburbs, and it was found that
they deteriorated in taste and in workmanship
so much that it was necessary to take mea-
sures to procure homes for them nearer their
work, The same result would follow the
driving out of the workmen from Clerkeuwell.
The contemplated new street from Old-street
to Bloomsbury, the making of which was the
immediate cause of this meeting, he believed
would be a failure. It would cause the
removal of many small houses without any
corresponding public benefit.
The motion was agreed to.
Dr. W. C. Bennett moved that a deputation
be appointed to wait on the Lord Mayor on the
subject. He said. the homes of the poor, not
only in London but in other large and small
towns, and the huts of the agricultural
labourers, were a disgrace to a Christian land,
and the wonder was that with the poor
under such influences society kept together at
all.
• Mr. Walker, of the Holborn Board of
Guardians, who seconded the resolution, com-
plained that the City Corporation had. not, as
they were bound to do by the Holborn Im-
provement Act, erected houses to replace those
taken down.
The resolution was agreed to; and a vote of
thanks to Sir John Bennett, and to Dr.
Bennett, who had occupied the chair dUring
the latter portion of the meeting, concluded
the proceedings.

articles.title: HYDE-PARK PROSECUTIONS.
articles.text:
THE HYDE-PARK PROSECUTIONS.

At the Marlborough-street Police Court on
Monday, Messrs. O'Leary, Bailey, Mooney,
O'Donnell, Odger, Osborne, Murray, Pottle,
Canham, Butler, and Clark were summoned
before Mr. Newton, for i&lawfully, and in
contravention of a certain regulation contained
in the first schedule annexed to an Act of
Parliament entitled" 'An Act for the Regula-
tion of the Royal Parks and Gardens,' to wit,
by delivering a certain public address in a
certain park called Hyde-park, not in accord-
ance with the rules of the said park, and con=
trary to the Statute, So."
Long before the hour fixed for the hearing
of the summonses—two o'clock—the approaches
and avenue of the court were crowded with
persons, chiefly belonging to the working-
class, and Messrs. Oder and Merriman were
loudly, cheered on their arriving at the court
from Mr. Scully's, the Grapes, Great Marl-
borough-street, where a sort of committee had
been sitting.
Mr. Poland, instructed by the Solicitor to
the Board of Works, prosecuted; and Mr.
Shackleton Hallett, barrister, appeared for
O'Leary and Mooney; and Mr. Baker Greene for
the others, both gentlemen being instructed
by Mr. J. J. Merriman.
On the names being called on, Mr. Newton.
said that one name would be sufficient, and
Mr. Bailey's summons was taken.
Mr. Baker Greene said he had, on several
grounds, to ask for an. adjournment, and he
believed his friend Mr. 'Poland would not
object to that course. Some of the summonses
had only been served on Saturday, and some
only that morning, and he had only been in-
structed on Saturday.
Mr. Poland said he could not, after whet
was statel by his learned friend, resist an
adjournment.
Mr. Shackleton Hallett said he was very
much in the position of his friend Mr. Baker
Greene, but he objected to the decision in Mr.
Bailey's case, as, if so, he would not have an
opportunity of addressing the Court in favour
of his client.
Mr. De Morgan, one of the defendants, said
he should defend himself, as also did Mr.
Odger, but objected to proceed on that day.
Mr. Newton adjourned the case for a week,
and said there was not to be any infringement
of the law, as it then stood, in the meantime.
The summonses were then adjourned.
On leaving Marlborough-street Police-court
on Monday afternoon, the persons summoned
proceeded with their friends to the Three
Doves publichouse, in Berwick-street, Soho.
Mr. Odger addressed the crowd outside from a
balcony, saying that he would go to prison
rather than pay a fine, lie knew that
"genteel reformers" regarded open air meet-
ings as vulgar things, but he did not lay claim to
belong to the genteel 'class of politicians. Mr.
Odger retired amid great cheering.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday the weekly meeting of this
Board took place at Guildhall, Lord Lawrence
in the chair.

Mr. Freeman, Chairman of the Finance
Committee, presented a balance-sheet of the
Board's income, expenditure, and liabilities
for the half-year ending 29th Sept., 1872, and
showing the details of such expenditure. Ho
moved that the document be now signed, and
that a discussion on it should be deferred till
the next meeting. Mr. Freeman thought that
the statement would satisfactorily rebut the
charge of extravagance which had been more
than once made against the Board. During
the last two years the Board had been expend-
ing a sum of money representing a rate of a
halfpenny in the pound. No doubt the Board
had borrowed a quarter of a million of money
from the Loan Commissioners, but only two
sums—namely, £15,000 and. £13,000—of that
amount had been obtained. -

The motion of Mr. Freeman was agreed to.
The income of the Board for the half-year
had been £95,408 19s id; and the expenditure
.C 77,839 fis 7d.
The Statistical Committee submitted the
result of their supplementary inquiry into the
condition of those schools which were reported
last year by the Government inspectors to be
only partially e cleat. It showed that,
whereas in March last the available elementary
school accommodation of London was reckoned
as sufficient for 350,920 children, it must now
be reduced to 330,734.
The debate on Mr. M‘Gregor's motion,
respecting the establishment of special schools
to meet special oases, was resumed, and in the
event a modified form of the original motion
was agreed to.

- Only nine cases came before the new Lord

at Saturday's show; and in six of these the
