CONFERENCE ON THE BALLOT.

On Thursday afternoon a conference was
oonvened at the Century Club, Pall Mall,
to promote an 'amendment of the Ballot
Act.
Mr. R. Marsden Latham, the president of
the Labour Representation League, who was
voted to the chair, denounced the present
system, and urged that in order to carry out a
real system of electoral reform the legal and ne-
cessary expenses of candidates would have to be
paid. Real protection must be given ,to the
voter, and the card system whieh had pre-
vailed, and which had entirely frustrated the
spirit of the Act, must be prohibited under
penalties. lie contendedt that the Ballot Act as
it stood did not secure electoral purity, neither
did it provide for an equitable distiibution of
electoral power. Ile introduced the subject in a
speech pointing out the defects of the Act,
and insisting that the efforts of the enemies of
Parliamentery reform could only be checked
by reopening the whole question. The Bill
should therefore proceed upon that principle.
Working men should have an opportunity of
recording their votes both at municipal and.
Parliamentary elections, without fear or in-
convenience. They could not talond to have
the labours of half a century, which had been
spent upon the Ballot, lost; and In order that
every one might be left to make up his own
mind, and exercise an unbiassed choice between
rival candidates, certain amendments and. ad-
ditions must be made to the Act. Paid agents
should be abolished altogether; it was al-
most impossible for a professional electioneering
agent to be an honest man, and if the
office could be done away with, nine-tenths
of the existing evils would disappear. Paid
canvassing Rhould also be declared illegal, and,
to facilitate, if not insure the direct repre-
sentation of labour, there should be equal
electoral constituencies, the county franchise
being assimilated to that of boroughs, and the
agricultural labourer freed from his present
miserably dependent state. The hours of poll-
ing must be extended to eight o'clock in the
evening, and candidates relieved of the legal
and official expenses of ele4ions. These
were some of the provisions it was proposed
to embody in the Bill, and if they could be
coupled with an easy, inexpensive, and effec-
tive registration of the voteps, the Ballot Act
might be made to accomplish the aim and
object of its sincerest advocates.
Mr. F. Young believed if the system of paid
agents was abolished as many votes would be
polled as now,' and they would be far more
independently recorded. He was also favour-
able to extending the hours of polling, which
could easily be accomplished if there were no
paid canvassers. With regard to the expenses
of elections he had no hesitation in saying

that if they were thrown upon the,ratepayers
they would be reduced to a minimum. In
conclusion he expressed a hope that the pre-
sent mode of registration would be much sim-
plified.
Mr. L. Jones considered the nation had
been plundered by a dishonest system of
elections, and reformers were anxious to
obtain an honest expression of the opinion of
the country. This was the great object of a
perfect ballot, because he did not look upon
the ballot as a principle. The Bill was passed,
but he did not believe the House of Commons
wished it to work, and the result was that
several of the leading Conservatives, by a kind
of legerdemain, were able to step in, and, as
it were, thwart the efforts which had been
made to secure an honest vote, He believed
if they could not put down the systems which
had cropped up under the Ballot Act they
would have the breaking of heads and all the
disturbances which had hitherto characterised
our elections, and which the ballot, it was
hoped, would 'prevent. All the working
()lasses required was that they should have
independent representation, and that wisp,
sooner or later, must be gratified.
Mr. Guile then moved the establishment of
a national association to secure the intro-
duction of a Bill to enact;—" 1. That any
violation or evasion of the secrecy of voting,
by whomsoever committed, either by the
collection of cards after polling, prying into
the ballot chamber, or otherwise, shall be
punished as a misdemeanour ; that any inter-
ferenoe with or molestation of an elector by a
canvasser or other person within a prescribed
distance from the polling booth, or during the
hours of polling, shall be punished as a mis-
demeanour; that if Parliament deem it im-
practicable to abolish paid agents altogether,
it shall nevertheless restrict as much as
possible the action of such persons at elections.
2. To relieve candidates of the public—that
is to say legal and official—expenses of elec-
tions, and to extend the hours of polling to
eight p.m. 3. To obtain the equalisation of
the franchise, and also such a simple method
of registration as will render it easy, inexpen-
sive, and effective."
Mr. Walton seconded the motion, which
' was carried.
Mr. G. Howell expressed his belief that they
would not get a real labour representation
until they had a redistribution of seats some-
thing similar to that which was proposed last
session by Mr. Walter Morrison M.P, This
would, he was sure, nullify the Morrison,
of tho

agents, and he also thought that there should
be a wider selection of candidates.

Mr. George Potter spoke of our Parlia-
mentary system as an anomaly and a disgrace.
The Government, he said, feared the working
classes if they were united, and were bound
to listen to them, and for that reason he
regretted the apathy that was exhibited. lie
considered it was idle to talk of the direct re-
presentation of labour so long as the working
men distrusted candidates of their own class,
or preferred a lord, a squire, or a capitalist,
who would subscribe to local institutions.
Until trades unions resolved to forego petty
internal jealousies he saw very little prospect
of working men getting justice from the Legis-
lature, or finding their way into Parliament.
Let trades unions interest themselves with
politics, disregarding temporary advantages in
' voting at the next general election, and the
benefit would be lasting instead of transitory,
as it was now, through the political apathy of
their members. -What minister could stand
against their organisation if it could be em-
ployed in political as well as domestic affairs?
(Cheers.)
The resolution was passed unanimously, and
a committee (on the motion of Sir John
Bennett) having been appointed to carry it
out, the proceedings closed with a vote of
thanks to the chairman for presiding.

An application was made on Tuesday to the
Court of Bankruptcy to register the resolution
passed by many of the creditors of Mr.
Frederick Strange, agreeing to aocept a com-
position of one shilling in the pound. On the
part of a dissentient creditor an objection was
made to the registration, on the -ground that
the deed was not in accordance with the
statute, because it provided for the payment of
a composition on a day which had long since
passed. Mr. Registrar Keene held the objed-
Con to be fatal.

Williams, or Barker, as the man is variously
named, who emulated the daring of Jack
Sheppard by breaking out of the Liverpool
Borough Gaol, has been sent for trial at the
Liverpool sessions. He says he did not know
that gaol-breaking was a felony.

On Tuesday morning a fire broke out in. the
beershop of Mr. H. Taylor, Midway-terrace,
Lower-road, Rotherithe. The house, a six
roomed. one, was much injured, and the ad-
joining shop of Mr. G. Record, boot and shoe
maker, was damaged.

A number of men were charged before the
Ashton magistrates on Monday with having
taken part in the recent violent demonstrations
against the Licensing Act. All of them were
committed for trial at the sessions,

Several firms in Sheffield are serious losers
by the Boston fire. Messrs. Butoher and Sons
cutlery manufacturers, Messrs. Jessop and
Sons, Brightside steel-works, have had their
establishments burned down, and it is feared
that the Boston stores of other American hawses
have shared a similar fate.

It was not until Monday that the bank of
the river Parrett, in Somersetshiro, which gave
way at Aller a fortnight ago, was repaired
suffloiently to prevent the continual now of the
tidal water which has submerged not only all
the moors but likewise the border lands for
miles around. Immense damage has been done
to the grazing lands, more particularly by the
sediment which the muddy water of the
Parrett will leave. The land. will be
drained by means of the engines and the Sedg-
moor main drain.

It is understood that the vacant judgeship
in the Court of Queen's Bench has been con-
fared upon Mr. Archibald, who, like Mr.
Justice Hannon, had never "taken silk."

Colston's Day at Bristol was on Wednesday
celebrated in the usual manner. Banquets
were held by both political parties in the city,
ann by two neutral societies, calling themselves
respectively the "Grateful" and the" Parent."
The Liberal gathering, which took place at
the New Theatre, excited much interest;
There were about 300 guests, including the
First Lord of the Admiralty, the Attorney-
General, Mr. Morley, 31,P., Lord Rollo,
Celonel Kingscote, M.P., Mr. Marling, M.P,
and Mr. E. A, Freeman, the eminent his-
torian.

Mr. Forster on Wednesday received a depu-
tation, whose members urged that teachers in
middle elass schools should be registered and
examined before their certificates were granted,
and that some council should be appointed
which should have control over such exami-
nation and registration. The right hon.
gentleman, in reply, pointed out that it was
to be considered how far the state of publio
business next session would allow any hope of
being able to pass such a measure as the depu-
tation suggested. He was sensible of the
.weight of the representations which had been
made, and his best attention should be given
to them.

THE BATTLE OF REFORM.
"Reform! Reform!" the people cry,
And not before Reform is needed ;

For true hearts bleed, and martyrs die,
Yet still their sufferings are unheeded.
Reform is wanted thro' the land, _

The workers' cry in tears ascendeth ;
Their rulers rule with iron hand,

And few the toiling class befriCndeth.
Reform! Reform! let's have Reform;

Up, up, brave champions, knights of labour!
Arm, arm yourselves, to meet the storm,
Unsheathe the two-edged moral sabre ;
And let our straight, unquav'ring blow,
Descend upon the heart that quaileth ;
March on, march !to meet the foe,
'Tis want and misery, if ye faileth.
Strike, strike the blow with dauntless hand !
And from our ranks out-weed the cowards ;
And who shall stop our giant-band P
Not all the blood of all the Tiowards !
March on, march on! in denser ranks,
Our flag for closer battle flying ;
March on, the foe is on our flanks,
Our numbers and our strength descrying.
March on, brave toilers for the right,
Our colours wave in triumph o'er us!
Alt, see, the foe quake at the sight!
Hurrah! they fly! they fly before us!
March onward, ever onward still,
"ris one wreath more bequeathed to story;
We'll gain the summit of the bill,
And strike again for England's glory.
JOHN ARTHUR. ELLIOTT.

THE FLOWERS FILLED WITH DEW.
Why do ye droop, sweet flowers?
Causing the crystals on your azure breasts,
To fall, in shattered beauty, from their bowers
To other nests.

Surely ye need not weep!
Yet diamond tear-drops fill your trembling
bells,
Like 'prisoned fays, in robes of light that sleep,
In perfumed cells.
Pale sorrow's blighting kiss
Cannot have pressed upon your infant brows ;
Nor can ye dwell on faded dreams of bliss,
Or broken vows.
Like one in whose torn heart

The depths of untold suffering are dry,
Who gazes on the tears that from ye start,
With yearning eye.

Perchance the mystics wind,
Your pensile chalices too roughly shakes;
The noisy blusterer should not be unkind,
For your sweet sakes.

Perchance the tear-drops fell,
From lovely Flora's dark cerulean eye;
She, weeping, thought how soon each pretty bell
, Must fade and die.

C. A. W.

articles.title: OLD HOUSE IN 8- STREET.
articles.text:
THE OLD HOUSE IN 8- STREET.

Not long ago there was an old house, in one of
our most filthy and noisy streets, which had not
been known to have one of its windows opened or
its doors unbarred for thirty years. The la ails had
become gray with old age, the glass in the window-
frames had all been broken out, and the shutters
spattered with mud. Never a light shone out from
It at night, never a step or voice was heard in it by
day. If by chance a venturesome urchin peeped
in at a keyhole, he shrank away, silent and chilled,
y the bare and mysterious solitude of the place.
No children sat upon its mildewed steps, mothers
quickened their pace as they passed it by, and
clasped their infants closer, for everyone had heard
that murder had been done within its walls, and
that upon its floor was a stain that had never come
out in all that time.

In those days, nearly forty years since, I was a
young and almost unknown lawyer, and, in fact,
nad never yet taken a brief, although a little pri-
vate practice had been given me. I used to feel a
little out of spirits at times on account of the slow
progress I was making, and got into a habit of
thinking life rather a tedious affair. Sitting one
i
evening n this frame of mind, and with a sort of
resigned air, counting the few shillings the day had
brought forth, I was startled by a low, hurried
knock at the door, and the quick entrance of a
young woman, closely 'veiled, though, as I saw
afterwards, of considerable beauty. She seemed
greatly agitated, and, handing her a chair, I was
obliged to wait until the words which her
trembling lips could hardly form, became intelli-
gible.
" Sir," said she, at length, "you are a lawyer;
I saw you in the court to-day—save hint, oh, save
him from certain, miserable, shameful death 1" '
I begged her to be calm and to be more ex-
plicit. I had, it was true, been in court that day,
and had seen part of a case which struck me as
odd, though I had not thought long upon the sub-
ject. It now seemed that I was to be made
acquainted with the particulars—which I condense
from the young woman's words and knowledge
afterwarda.gathered.

--
Silas Tliinnton--3.vas a wealthy old man, living
alone in ft house in 8 otrest. Ile was a moan

and sordid miser, whose whole heart and soul and
strength were centred in the love of money—a
love that had driven out of him almost every
human feeling, and made him starve his wife, drive
his son out of doors, rob if he could safely, grind
the poor, crawl to the rich, and become hated,
despised, and feared by every being with whom
he had to do. I said he was alone. But an old
woman kept his house for him—a toothless,
wrinkled, crouching old creature, whose bleared
eyes seemed to have lost every spark of intelli-
gence, and whose mumbling voice never formed a
word that man could understand. But she looked
all the doors when her master was out, ate nothing
apparently, never bought clothes, but wore the old
rags, was deaf and could hear no secrets, was near
dumb and could tell none. She used to sit, cower-
ing over the nearly cold stove, night and day, until
one might have wondered whether the bundle of
rigs she was, was alive or dead. There was a son,
too—a wild, open-hearted fellow enough, and as
generous, doubtless, as his father was avaricious.
Such ahome was no place for him, and he had
gone away years before to sea, leaving behind,
with many tears and lover's vows, a young girl—
she who sat before me now.

Upon an evening in that week the son had
suddenly and unexpectedly returned from sea. It
was stated by the neighbours who saw him that
he made his appearance in the evening, and that,
after knocking at the door for some time, hs was
admitted, only after some hesitation, by the old
woman. Certainly the prospect was not very
cheering for him, as, when he had before darkened
that portal, he had been bidden never to return.
The engagement to the young girl was alone
reason enough of discord in the old man's mind,
he fearing that he might be called upon to pro-
vide for his son's household, And now he was
almost obliged to force himself into his father's
presence, uncertain whether he would not imme-
diately be thrust forth. Nothing more was said of
the young man's appearance, as the door was not
seen to open again. And with some few specula-
tions as to the reception the ' old miser would
extend to his son, and criticisms upon his rough
and •uncouth bearing, the neighbours went about
their business.

Next day there was a rumour that something
was wrong in the old man's house. Long
after the hour when the shutter of the room
where the old man often set was usually
opened, it remained closed. This in itself, one
would think, need have excited no actual alarm,
but there was something so uncommon in his
habits that he was more closely watched than
other people. There was an undefined feeling
that something was wrong. None eould tell how
or why, but a sort of dread began to creep over
people; and by the middle of the day quite a crowd
had gathered in front of the house, scrutinizing
the windows, and talking in whispers of the
miser and his son's return. The policeman, how-
ever, would not take any steps to see if anything
was amiss, and so the day passed over. But next
day the mystery became unbearable; and a few
bold spirits burst the door open, and entered the
house. But the boldest of them walked gently,
and peered anxiously before them, as they saw
what a dreary, tomb-like place they had invaded.
And their minds were almost prepared to find, as
they did, the old man dead on the floor in his
MOM.

Hu had been dead many hours. As he lay on
his face, the blood from his battered head and
gashed throat stood in congealed pools about him.
The place was in great disorder, but there were
no evidences of any struggle. He had evidently
been struck down where he sat, and then the
murder completed as he lay insensible. His keys
were in his pockets, and upon his desk a cash-box
lay untouched, as were many articles of value
stowed away in strong boxes. Upon the floor was
a heavy and formidable walking-staff, its head
smeared with blood and hair. Where was the old
woman P She was found in the kitchen, in her
old attitude—nor did she utter a word when
questioned. And where was the son? Ho was
not in the house; but the stick was the same
that a score of people had seen in his hand when
he knocked at his father's door not many hours
before!

Police regulations were not so perfect then as
they are now, but it was not long before the son
was captured. He was found walking with his
sweetheart, and both were locked up. He
struggled hard at first; but she begged him not
to drive the officers to use force, and he submitted,
saying that they should pay for detaining him.
But his heart sank when he was told of the charge,
and of the evidence furnished by the club and his
visit to his father, as well as by the notoriously
bad terms on which they had lived. When, too,
left for the night in darkness, the full reality of
his danger rose before his mind, and he was cowed.
The girl had been set free—there was no need to
shut her up in prison—but with the first blush of
morning she was back, begging to be let in to him
to take whose life was to kill her. Next day the
young man was committed for trial, as was in-
evitable, and it was upon the evening of that day
that his sweetheart came to me, as I have already
described.

These being the facts, I saw that they presented
much difficulty. Whether the young man was
guilty or not, none but One above knew—unless
indeed the wretched piece of humanity who lived
with the murdered man could tell anything, or
knew anything to tell. Perhaps the worst circum-
stance in the case was that a man who lived next
door heard loud voices about an hour after the son
had been let into the house. Ono voice was that
of the old man, the other that of the prisoner, who
seemed to speak as if highly exasperated. The
sound had ceased suddenly, and soon afterwards the
hack door was opened, as he know by the sound,
and he heard heavy steps passing down the passage
leading thence into another street.

Rearier, I honestly told the weeping girl that
the evidence looked black, and that, though I
would do my best for her lover, I feared the worst.
For the present she must leave me; I would
collect my thoughts.

I sat in my room hour after honr, revolving this
strange deed in my mind; but the longer I thought
the more I feared that, though the murder was
most likely unpremeditated, it might have been
the result of passion called forth by the sense of
old wrongs and present harshness. At last, how-
ever, I decided upon my plan of action, and pro-
ceeded to carry it out forthwith.

In the first place, I visited the prisoner. Al-
though my youthful faith in the science of physi-
ognomy had been much shaken by many cases in
which innocent faces had given the lie to black
hearts which had brought youth and age together
side by side in the courts which I frequented, I
was anxious to study the face and manner of this
youth. I wished to believe him innocent I
should work all the better, perhaps; and if his face
seemed ruffianly or treacherous I should certainly
work none the less heartily, for it was my first
criminal case. He was sitting down as I entered,
but rose immediately, and, stepping forward
promptly, offered his band frankly, like a man.
I 'took it as promptly; the action seemed to show
that no stain of blood was upon it. And as I re-
marked the cheerful though serious manner in
which he spoke of his position, and the broken
voice in which he hoped God would be good to him
for his poor Mary's sake, I found my eyes becom-
ing dim, and felt a rising choke in my throat.
His story was this. As I knew before, he had
just returned from seven years at sea. Money he
had acquired, and did not intend to ask his father
for any. His sole object, as he said, was to make
peace; and if he could not gain a hearty consent
to his long-postponed marriage, at least to know
that it had become a matter of little interest to the
old man. Absence, too, had obliterated or softened
down much of the asperity with which he had
left home; like many others, when he fell among
strangers he had yearned for the bare, comfortless
home of his young days. Trying to blame him-
self and to excuse his father for muoh that had
passed between them, he turned his steps towards
the old house, with something like love for his
parent stirring in his heart. He knocked at the
door, timidly at first, and then long and loudly.
At last a slow, shuffling step came along the echo-
ing passage, and lock after lock, and bolt after bolt
being slowly unfastened, the well-remembered face
of the old woman peered forth from the still
chained door.

"I want to see my father," said he.
And the old woman, locking the door upon him,
again shuffled back with his message. Thrice was
it disregarded, and thrice the son begged to be let
in; and at last he was conducted into the prison-
like room of his father. The old man did not
raise his eyes from his account-book for some time.
At last, slowly closing the book, putting his spec-
tacles carefully into their case, and thrusting both
hands into his pookete, he suddenly wheeled round
in his chair, and in his harshest tones demanded
what the young man wanted.
"Nothing," was the reply.
"Then why come here " was the loving re-
sponse.
"I thought you might like to see your son,"
was the answer to this greeting.
"No, I would that I should never see your face
again. Go!" said his father.
The young man tried long and earnestly to
soften his father's heart towards him, but to no
purpose. Old Thornton only grew exasperated,
and began to shout and swear at his son as if
possessed.
"Be off! travel! You're like your mother,
with her baby face and spaniel's whining! Travel,
I say! or I'll beat this book about your head, old
as I am ! "

And so the son saw that his home was never to
be reopened to him, his father never to be a parent
to him, and he turned to go.
"Father," said he, as he stood for the last time
upon the threshold, "You think I come for money
—I know you love it—but Ido not. Shall I come
again to-morrow ? "
"Look here! " said Silas, with a quiet grin, "I
hate you—l hated your mother—l hate everybody
—and I love gold; it's the only friend a man has.
If you say you don't covet it, you lie! I'll keep
it till I die ; and then, if old Madge is alive, she
shall have it all; if she's dead, I'll bury it twenty
yards deep, if these old hands can do the job."
Young Thornton left the room without another
word. As he did so, he was surprised to see that
old Madge had been listening; but she seemed so
mummy-like that he did not think of it. She
was so insensible to his voice that she would not
open the front door for him, and he departed by
the back door, as he had done hundreds of times
when a boy. And that was all my client knew of
the last days of Silas Thornton as he protested to
me with tears in his eyes, and, I thought, truth
in every tone and look._

I bade the prisoner be of good cheer, though
my heart misgave me as I thought of the difficul-
ties with which he was surrounded; and I left him.
The first step was to secure the old womin ; that
had already been done, and she was safe in the
House of Detention. The next was to see her,
which lat once proceeded to do. To my surprise,
she presented a very different appearance from
that which she had worn on the preliminary of the
trial of the day before. Then she was insensible
to sound or look; now she seemed vivacious, and
eager almost to, converse on the dreadful subject.
After some general observations, she asked where
Master Henry (the prisoner) was P I told her.
"Did my master make a will ?" said she.
"Not that I know of',"
said I; "but you should
know all about that."
And I put into my face a look of confidential
friendship.
"Ay,
,true, true, true," she absently returned:

this, and it has. I haven't studied it over so long
for nothing. Good, good, good for old Madge!

that ? "

- I -did mind that, and I told her so, but with a
smile of approval that made me blush as I put it
on.

"Yes," whispered she, with a chuckle between
the words, "I'm his heir. Look here, Mister
Lawyer! You're young and fond of pleasure,
ain't you? I was once. Well, I shall want a
young lawyer, fond of pleasure, and poor—d'ye
mark me? poor—in a few days. Ha, ha! When
old Thornton's buried, and that cub of a son of
his hung, come to me, lawyer—l shall want you.
D'ye mind me? I shall be rich; you are poor,
poor—young men always are—it'b only old men
and women that get rich. But be sure and wait "
—and the old hag thrust her wrinkled face olose
to mine—" wait till old Thornton's buried, and
his cub of a son hung."
This strange talk startled me much, for it might
be the raving of madness or the babbling of age.
She ceased talking, however, after this outburst,
nor could I obtain a particle of evidence exculpat-
ing the son. The only thing I could get out of
her was either vacant looks, or a hideous grin, and
a gesture of secrecy, or a whisper to "wait."

Silas Thornton was buried, and the preparations
for trying whether his son should be hung came
on swiftly. I had not a particle more evidence
to offer. The old woman had again relapsed into
silence, and would not speak to a soul. Nothing
could be brought forward in the prisoner's favour,
while against him stood the damning facts of the
stick, the ill.will, the quarrel, and the apparently
secret exit from the house. And so the trial came
on.

I pass over the many agonizing interviews be-
tween the prisoner and the young girl. Why de-
scribe them F The walls of every prison cell have
at times given back dull echoes of father's, mo-
ther's, lover's, or sister's grief, poured out before
loved but lost ones, the secrets of whose hearts are
known but to Him who is the panther of hearts.
Ah! there is many a fountain,Of love opened by
the stroke of mistintune, which would have proved
a well-spring of life if unsealed earlier, and while
the young and,untried spirit was blindly seeking
for the promised land.
And so the trial came on.

It was a fair day, and the solemn aspect of the
court seemei almost wicked, I thought, in the face
of nature's loveliness. It should have been a day
of clouds and storms upon which to try a man for
his life. "Henry Thornton," at length said the
clerk, and the prisoner was brought in. At the
same moment a heavy staff, stained with hair and
blood, was laid on the clerk's table, and a plan of
the miser's house placed beside it. An object done
up in rags almost, it seemed, was propped up in a
corner of the witness-box, and people wondered
what it could be. A slender form, also, drooped
at my side dressed in black, and people knew tha
it was the prisoner's betrothed. He himself saw
all, and a shade of doubt—not fear--Thissed over
him. But a veil was raised for a moment, and
from the face under it shone out such a beam of
sunlight that the shadow vanished and he sat
down. Hundleds saw the look, and hundreds
said under their breath, "how young they both
look ! "

_
The first, second, third, and fourth witnesses
were called. They had to prove the knocking and .
admittance of the young man, and to identify the
stick. They all did it clearly; and the prisoner
said, with a bow, that what they had said was
true. _

Then came the man next door, who had heard
quarrelling, as he thought, and the footsteps
leaving the hue° by the back way. His testi-
mony was admitted, also, by the prisoner, as cor-
rect in every particular. There were loud voices;
they were those of his father and himself; he did
go away by the back door.
Next came the evidence of the police, and these
who first entered the house. All was clear. Even
their testimony was unquestionable—the stick did
belong to the prisoner.
Next came the old woman. She was, or pre-
tended to be, perfectly imbecile and as deaf as a
post, and was soon told to stand down. As she
turned to go out of the box, "Oh, he is lost, he is
lost! "sobbed the girl at my side, and "He is lost!
said in effect an awe-struck murmur round the
court.
But neither the girl, nor the prisoner, nor the
Judge, nor the people saw the glance which the old
woman threw at me. I arose calmly, as one who
feels power within him.
"One word more, Madge," said I, very gently,
and she calm) back. " The prisoner seemed agi-
tated when he came in at the door, didn't he,
Aladge "
" He was mad with his father for keeping him
waiting," she promptly responded.
Every breath in court was held, and the judge
took a dip of ink as he stared to see this sudden
making of the dumb to speak.
"Did they quarrel at all Madge, when he came
in P "

"All the time he was there, " said she.
Well—just so—it's important to prove that they
quarrelled, you, see, Madge. How do you know
that they quarrelled all the time? said I in my
blandest tones.

" Because I listened, said she," with a sort of
sly laugh.
"Why did you litn, Madge ?—did you fear
mischief P"

"Yes, I not only fearel but I knew What WO
coming; but—but—oh yes! I remember I went
away down stairs before it was done, don't you
understand, lawyer l'—before it was done."
" Now,.Madge, one more question, and that is
Don't be alarmed; it's only one question:
When old Thornton w ts down on tlt) door—"
"Ay, he was d.iwn on th floor," said she.
"With his head stuashed in with that stick—
added I.

"That stick— smashed in; yes; that was it
she replied, almc•st fa a whisper.

"Are you listening, Madge ?" added I, softly--
very softly.
"Yes, yes; go on; I hear every word. He's
young and poor—poor," she said, vacantly.
"Then," shouted I, with all my power; "then
what did you do with the knife you cut his throat
with ?"
Could that thing have been human whiult fell
in a heap upon the floor, and tore and plucked at
itself, and shrieked and yelled? It was no fiend;
it was old Madge, whose words thrilled through
the court.
"I killed him! I killed him! I killed him!
Look up the chimney. Ha, ha! I was too clever
for him! What did he promise to marry me for,
forty years ago? What did be starve me for?
What did he curse me for every day? He said
he'd make a lady of me; so he has—l've got his
money; and I knocked his bead, and I cut his
throat, and I'd have torn his old face if I hadn't
kissed it many a time, forty years ago."
Raving thus she was carried out of court, while
the crowd sent up shout after shout of gladness;
and the prisoner— a prisoner no longer—took a
fainting form in his arms, and begged the people
to give her air for God's sake!
Old Madge lived some years after this, a perfect
lunatic. Never once did a ray of intellect, again
illumine that aged face. There were some who
pitied her, and said that sho may have loved the
man she murdered, and anyhow it was certain that
he had not used her well. But most people forgot
all about her and the miser's death; and the old
house was the only token left of the horrible
deed.

articles.text:
OUR MISCELLANY.

WHY SHOULD ANY MAN SWEAR?
I can conceive of no reason why he should, but
ten reasons why be should not.
1. It is mean. A man of high moral standing
would almost as soon steal a sheep as swear.
2. It is vulgar : altogether too low for a decent
man.
3. It is cowardly: implying a fear either of not
being believed or obeyed.
4. Itis ungentlemanly. A gentleman, acoording
to Webster, Is a genteel man—well-bred, refined.
Such an one will no more swear than go into the
street to throw mud with a chimney-sweep.
6. it is indecent: offensive to delicacy, and ex-
tremely unfit for human ears.
6. It is foolish. "Want of decency is want of

sense."
7. It is abusive—to the mind which conceives
the oath, the tongue which utters it, and to the
person at whom it is aimed.
8. It is venomous—showing a man's heart to be
a nest of vipers; and every time he swears, one of
them sticks out of his bead.
9. It is contemptible—forfeiting the respect of
all the wise and good.
10. It is wicked—violating the Divine law, and
provoking the displeasure of Him who will not hold
him guiltless who takes His name in vain.

A BENEVOLENT METHOD OF SERVING

ONE'S SELF.

An Italian gentleman, with great sagacity, de-
vised a very productive pump, and kept it in action
at little expense. The garden wall of his villa
adjoined the great high road leading from one of
the capitals of Northern Italy, from which it was
distant but a few miles. Possessing within his
garden a fine spring of water, he erected on the
outside of the wall a pump for public use; and
chaining to it a small iron ladle, he placed near it
some rude seats for the weary traveller, and by a
slight roof of climbing plants protected the whole
from the mid-day sun. In this delightful shade
the tired and thirsty travellers on that well-beaten
road, ever and anon reposei and refreshed them-
selves, and did not fail to put in requisition the
services which the pump so opportunely presented
to them. From morning till night, many a dusty
and way-worn pilgrim plied its handle, and went
on his way, blessing the liberal proprietor for his
kind consideration of the passing stranger. But
the owner of the villa was deeply acquainted with
human nature. He knew that in that sultry
climate the liquid would be more valued from its
scarcity, and front the difficulty of acquiring it.
He, therefore, in or& r to enhance tho value of the
gift, wisely arranged the pump, so that its spout
was of rather contracted dimensions, and the
handle required a moderate application of force to
work it. Under these circumstances, the pump
raised far more water than could pass through its
spout; and, to prevent its being wasted, the surplus
was conveyed by an invisible channel to a large,
reservoir judiciously placed for watering the pro-
prietor's own house, stables, and garden, into
which about five plats were pouted for every
spoonful passing out of the spout for the benefit of
the weary traveller. Even this latter portion was
not entirely neglected, for the waste pipe conveyed
the part which ran over from the ladle, to some
delicious strawberry beds at a lower level. Per-
haps, by a small addition to this benevolent
arrangement, some kind-hearted travellers might
be induced to indulge their mules and asses with a
taste of the same cool and refreshing fluid, thus
paying an additional tribute to the skill and
sagacity of the benevolent proprietor.

THE UNFORTUNATE CIPHER.
A merchant at Marseilles, having a businem
correspondent on the African coast, bethought him,
that as some members of his family had shown a
partiality for monkeys, he might gratify them by
sending for one or two specimens of these animals
from Africa. Accordingly he wrote to his corre-
spondent to procure two or three of the finest and
most admired species, and transmit them to Mar-
seilles. Chance so ordered it that the merchant,
in putting down the ou (in English or) between
the figures 2 and 3, made the o very prominent,
while the u remained scarcely visible. Same
months afterwards a ship porter came in all haste
to the old merchant, and announced to him that
his menagerie had:arrived. " Menagerie!" cried
the merchant. "Yes, a menagerie, a whole cargo
of monkeys had arrived to his consignment."
The merchant could scarcely credit the announce-
ment, until the letter of his correspondent was put
into his hands. In that .epistle the African
negotiant, a man of the most uncompromising
exactitude, excused himself very earnestly for not
having been able, with all his exertions, to procure
more than 160 monkeys in place of the 203
ordered, but promised, as soon as possible, to fulfil
the entire demand. The feelings of the honest
merchant may be guessed when, on moving down
to the quay to satisfy himself on the subject by
()cider inspection, he beheld his 160 monkeys, all
duly caged and littered, and grinning at him with
the most laudable pertinacity. It was the moment
when a man might reasonably doubt whether it
would be hest to laugh or cry. So much for the
value of ciphers.

it is the petty vexatious, the small jealousies, the

make the heart heavy and the temper sour. Don't

THE BISHOP OF GLOUCESTER T,

THE ATTORNEY-GENERAL
To the Editor of the BEz-HivE.

SlR,—The Bishop of Gloucester reproves the
Attorney-General for having grossly failed in
his conduct of the late Tichborne trial in the
following words :—" When a man, even in his
own craft and calling, so badly managed a
grave case as to make a person like him who
was called "The Claimant" become a kind of
hero, and by the use of strong language and
even offensive language, obtained for him a
kind of sympathy, such a gentleman had better
by far look to matters at home in his own
religious life, and leave dukes' and. bishops'
alone."

But might not the people reprove the Bishop
for having grossly mismanaged the teaching
of Christianity, in the following words
"When a body of men, even in their own
craft and calling, so badly mismanage a grave
case as to make a person like him, who was
called "the prophet of Nazareth" become a
kind of God, and by the use of strong, and
even offensive language (see Athanasian Creed)
obtained for him a kind of worship (although
it was his Father and our Father that he would
alone have had men worship and not himself)
such gentlemen had better by far look to
matters at home in their own relations of life,
and leave the Government alone to educate the
people.
T. G. HEADLEY.

THE UNITED KINGDOM SOCIETY OF
COACHMAKERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—Seeing in your paper an extract from
our last report, likewise a letter from a mem-
ber at Torquay, allow me to give your
readers some idea of that society. There is
a rule which states any member going on
travel must first bring a note from the shop
secretary, stating the reasons of his leaving
his employment. This rule is never enforced;
any member losing his employment through
drunkenness or idleness can at any time have
his card, and no enquiries made; if any mem-
ber falls out of employment, he has to travel
for is. ad. a day and bed, unless he has been
a paying member for ten successive years.
This system has been the ruin of many a man
who might have been a useful member of
society. It likewise upholds the piecemasters'
system in all its blackness in the railv..ay
shops, and in the towns where the system
exists, as the officers and committee are either
piecemasters, or favourite men of piecemast-rs.
Should a man speak his mind, he is sure to
be spotted. We, the men of Miles Platting
London and Yorkshire Railway Works, have
been trying to pass a rule to bear on the
piecemasters' system, and we have had every
obstacle placed in our way both by the execu-
tive at Liverpool and by the private men and
officers in Manchester. Last Thursday night,
being the night for the alterations of rules,
ours were thrown out, so we have to go back
for another three years to a state of slavery
and bondage, and pay 9d. a week to uphold
it, and then we have for our motto "Trium-
phant we. Bravely Defend." . I think it ought
to be oppress instead of defend; and as I.
guarantee this statement to be correct, I send
you my name.—Yours,
GEORGE TOOGOOD,
Coach-body Maker.

EMIGRATION OF FARM LABOURER

TO SOUTH AMERICA,

The Pacific Steamship Company's royal Mail
steamer Lttsitania, which sailed from Liverpool
on Wednesday for Valparaiso and other South
American ports, had on board fifty farm
labourers, chiefly from the neighbourhood of
Leamington, Gloucester, &a., who go out to
Rio de Janeiro under the auspices of the
National Agricultural Labourers' Union. It
appears that Mr. Alsop, who is one of the
principal promoters of the Union, and who
has just returned to England from Brazil, is
now engaged, at the request of the Emperor
of Brazil, in sending out agricultural labourers
from the districts above mentioned, for* the
purpose of teaching the Brazilians "good
farming" on the English settlement at Cananea,
where there are at present 114 labourers em-
ployed. The Emperor has already appointed a
governor, a clergyman, a schoolmaster, and
police, for the embryo capital of the new colony,
which lies ten miles inland from the port of
Cananea.
The emigrants on arriving at Rio will be
forwarded at once to their destination; £2 per
head (to those over 10 years of age) is presented
to them on settling, and 2s. a day allowed,
with seeds and tools, until the first crop is
reaped. The purchase money, a nominal sum,
and the cost of the passage, £ll, being 'repay-
able in instalments. Three hundred acres can,
it is stated, be bought for £25.

GNNTLEMEN,—One of the duties which devolved
tpon us, as the Parliamentary Committee ap-

drawing up of Standing Orders for the better
despatch of business at all future Congresses.
In accordance with the instructions then received

earnestly requesting that trades societies and

It is necessary to be borne in mind that these

speak, so that those who from time to time identify

to give advice or aid in the great work to which
we have addressed ourselves.
With these limitations, which have become
expedient, not in an exclusive spirit, but in conse-
quence of the many important questions to which
we must from time to time devote our attention,
we believe that these annual Labour Parliaments
will materially aid in giving tone and coherence

greatly help us in getting such enabling laws

6. A. committee of three shall be elected to
examine the credentials, and report thereon to the
meeting.

7. The delegates shall then proceed, to elect the
President of the Congress, preference being given
to a delegate of the town where the Congress is
being held.

8. The Congress shall then elect a Secretary, a I
like preference being given.
9. The Congress shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent,,a door-keeper .and a messenger.
10. A standing committee of live shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The vice-president
to be the chairman a the committee.
11. After the routine business of election of
officers and committee, the president shall formally
open the Congress with an address.
12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of business, with perfect
fairness to all who have been to the trouble to
prepare papers, of which duo notice has been
given, shall have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion.
13. The standing committee shall be allowed to
retire at 4 o'clock each day (one hour before
°losing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.
14. Each delegate-shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10s. towards
the expenses of the Congress; and in Me he
represents more than one socity, 10s. for every
such society he is delegated to represent. The
names of these who have, and those who have not
paid, to be read over when the roll is called on the
following morning. No person shall be deemed a
member of Congress until his levy is paid.
15. The reader of a paper shall be allowed
twenty minutes; the mover of a resolution fifteen
minutes; succeeding speakers ten minutes each;
no one shall speak more than once on any one
question. After the reply, no one shall be allowed
to speak on the question before the chair, but it
shall be at once put to the vote by the chairman.
16. No second amendment, or rider to an ori-
ginal proposition, shall be put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.
17. The voting shall be by show of hands; but
in case of a dispute, the chairman may order a
division.

18. Two tellers shall be appointed by the Conc.
gress, and their ruling shall be final.
19. If more than one amendment is proposed,
the standing committee may retire, together with
the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers' of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
21. In the selection of papers to be read, pre-
ference shall be given to those of which notice has
been given, and in the order in which they have
been received by the committee.
22. Subjects having special reference to the
trade of the town or locality where the Congress
is being held, shall in rio case be allowed to oc-
cupy the time of more than one sitting of the
congress. And it is desirable that these special
subjects be laid before the committee as early as
practicable, for the purpose of arranging them
under one or two general heads, and embodying
them in one or two simple propositions.
23. No delegate shall leave the room without
the consent of the Vice-President: and delegates
absent ono whole sitting without leave of absence,
shall be named by the Chairman.
24. A General or Parliamentary Committee of
nine shall be elected on the last day of each Con-
gress, who shall continue in office until they
are re-elected, or their successors are appointed.
They shall clout from among themselves a
President, Treasurer, and Secretary for the
ensuing. year; and they also shall remain in
office until they are re-elected, or their successors
are appointed.
25. All surplus monies after payment of the
expenses of the Congress, ;hall be handed over to
the Treasurer of the Parliamentary Committee for
the general purposes of such Committee.
26. The duties of the Parliamentary Com-
raittee shall be (1) to watch ,all legislative
measures directly affecting the questions of labour,
and (2) to initiate, whenever necessary, such
legislative action as Congress may direct, or as the
exigencies of the time and circumstances may
demand.

27. The officers, under the direction of the
committee, shall have authority to solicit sub-
scriptions, donations, or levies, for the purpose of
defraying the expenses incurred by such com-
mittee; but the mode of payment shall be left
optional with each society as to whether it shall
pay by levy or donation.
28. The Congress having been formally opened
by the President, after tho usual routine business
of electing officers and committee, the Parlia-
mentary Committee shall present their report for
the past year, which shall be read by the Parlia-
mentary Secretary, and shall lay it on the table
for discussion by the Congress.
29. The Parliamentary Committee shall assist
and co-operate with the local committee of the
town where the next Congress is to be held, for
the purpose of making the arrangements as com-
plete as possible, and preparing the questions to
be discussed, and together to take such joint action
as the business or other special circumstances of
the time may render necessary or desirable.
30. The Parliamentary Committee, in conjunc-
tion with the local committee, shall be empowered
to invite persons to attend the sittings of the Con-
gress whose presence they may deem advisable
and desirable such persons to be allowed to
address the desirable,
on the invitation of the
